MetallurgyInorganic Chemistry • JEE Advanced

01 Foundations of metallurgy

1.1 Mineral, ore and gangue

1.1.1 Mineral

A mineral is a naturally occurring substance with characteristic composition and physical properties. Metallic elements commonly occur in the Earth's crust in minerals containing oxides, sulphides, carbonates, halides, silicates and other compounds.

1.1.2 Ore

An ore is a naturally occurring mineral deposit from which a metal can be extracted economically and conveniently with available technology. Every ore contains mineral matter, but every mineral is not an ore. This distinction is economic and technological, not simply chemical.

Example — iron pyrites: Pyrite (FeS2), also called fool's gold, contains iron but is generally not preferred as an iron ore. It has high sulphur content. Residual sulphur can make iron brittle, and its removal adds an unnecessary processing burden. The oxide can nevertheless be formed and reduced in principle.

4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2

Example — copper pyrites: Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) contains iron and sulphur but is a major commercial copper ore because copper can be concentrated and extracted profitably.

1.1.3 Gangue or matrix

Gangue is unwanted earthy, rocky or mineral material associated with the valuable ore mineral. It may be silica, silicates, clay, limestone, unwanted oxides or other sulphides. It is not restricted to soil.

1.2 General metallurgical route

  1. Crushing and grinding: liberate the valuable mineral grains from the gangue matrix.
  2. Concentration (beneficiation or ore dressing): separate as much gangue as practical.
  3. Conversion: convert the concentrate to a suitable extractable compound, often an oxide by calcination or roasting.
  4. Reduction or metal winning: obtain the elemental metal from its compound by a suitable chemical or electrolytic route.
  5. Refining: remove residual impurities to obtain the required purity.

Not all ores require this exact sequence. Certain noble metals may be leached directly, whereas highly electropositive metals require specialised routes, usually molten-salt electrolysis. Stages may be skipped, combined or reordered.

Why the sequence can change: noble metals may be dissolved and recovered without first roasting to oxides. Highly electropositive metals are recovered from anhydrous molten electrolytes. The form of the concentrate determines which conversion and reduction steps are necessary.

1.3 Selection of ore concentration method

The method is selected by a significant difference between the valuable mineral and the gangue, rather than by the name of the ore alone.

MethodProperty exploitedTypical application
Gravity separation / hydraulic washingDensity and settling behaviourDense cassiterite, iron oxides or chromite with lighter gangue
Magnetic separationMagnetic responseOne fraction magnetic, the other non-magnetic
Froth flotationSurface wettabilityMainly sulphide ores
LeachingSelective chemical solubilityBauxite, gold/silver, low-grade copper ores

1.3.1 Decision-making examples

If a useful density contrast exists, choose gravity separation. If one fraction is magnetic, choose magnetic separation. If a sulphide mineral can be selectively made hydrophobic, use froth flotation. If selective dissolution or complexation is available, use leaching.

Worked example — Choose the concentration method
Cassiterite mixed with lighter quartz: gravity separation. Cassiterite mixed with magnetic wolframite: magnetic separation. Galena mixed with siliceous gangue: froth flotation. For bauxite, the useful aluminium-bearing component is selectively dissolved in alkali; hence chemical concentration. The same ore may require more than one method.

Ore identification and method selection are different tasks. Pyrolusite (MnO2), dolomite (CaCO3·MgCO3), chromite (FeCr2O4), colemanite (Ca2B6O11·5H2O), siderite (FeCO3), anglesite (PbSO4), cerussite (PbCO3), chalcocite (Cu2S) and atacamite (Cu2Cl(OH)3) illustrate different mineral classes. Knowing the formula alone does not establish whether gravity, magnetic, flotation or chemical separation is appropriate. See the complete ore atlas.

1.4 Gravity separation, hydraulic washing and levigation

1.4.1 Principle

Gravity separation exploits the difference in density (specific gravity) and settling behaviour between the desired mineral and the gangue. A moving water stream carries lighter grains away more readily, while denser grains settle or are retained. The method is often used for oxide ores, but the deciding condition is a sufficient density and settling-velocity contrast, not the oxide character.

1.4.2 Hydraulic washing

Finely crush or powder the ore to liberate its grains. Treat the liberated particles with a controlled stream of running water. Lighter gangue is washed away, whereas the heavier mineral is collected as concentrate. Control of particle size, liberation and water velocity is essential. In an upward flow, fine/light particles are carried upward more easily; coarse/dense particles tend to settle.

ExampleFormulaReason for suitability
CassiteriteSnO2Dense oxide separable from lighter siliceous gangue
Iron oxide ores, e.g. haematiteFe2O3Useful density difference with siliceous gangue
ChromiteFeCr2O4Dense mineral amenable to gravity treatment in a suitable feed

Why the separation occurs: Water carries suspended particles. The comparatively heavy, liberated ore grains settle more readily than light gangue grains of comparable size. A very fine heavy grain can behave like a larger light grain; therefore crushing, sizing and control of water flow are important.

Worked example — Concentrate grade and recovery
A 100 kg feed contains 20 kg of valuable mineral. A 30 kg concentrate contains 18 kg of that mineral. Concentrate grade = (18/30) × 100 = 60%; recovery = (18/20) × 100 = 90%. The tailings still contain 2 kg of valuable mineral.

1.4.3 Wilfley shaking table

A Wilfley table is a slightly inclined deck with raised strips, corrugations or riffles. The table continuously vibrates or reciprocates. A controlled cross-flow of water moves across its surface.

  1. Feed the finely divided ore onto the inclined deck.
  2. Water carries lighter particles across the deck.
  3. Vibration causes particles to stratify: dense grains remain nearer the deck and riffles guide or hinder their movement, while lighter grains are displaced farther by the water.
  4. Collect the dense fraction and lighter tailings separately.

Sequence on the shaking table: The feed is supplied near the upper end of the inclined table. A water film moves across the table while the shaking motion moves the bed along the riffles. Denser particles settle close to the table surface and are retained behind the riffles; lighter particles move across the riffles with the water. The riffles and inclination are adjustable. Collect the heavy concentrate and light tailings separately, continuously.

1.4.4 Stratification and riffle loading

The riffles exploit the different hydraulic behaviour of heavy and light grains. Dense material is concentrated in the lower layers; the lighter material is washed away. Continuous removal of the heavy fraction is essential. If dense grains accumulate excessively behind riffles, the bed overloads. Heavy and light grains may then pass over barriers together and separation efficiency decreases. Riffle height and geometry, inclination, vibration and feed rate must match the ore.

Effect of excessive loading: a riffle retains the lower, heavy layer only while its height and the water stream are compatible with the feed. As the heavy bed rises above the effective riffle height, light and heavy grains can spill together. A continuous concentrate discharge is therefore part of the separation mechanism, not just a collection convenience.

Worked example — Riffle loading and water flow
If too much dense concentrate is allowed to accumulate behind the riffles, lighter and heavier grains can eventually pass over the barriers together. Adjusting the feed rate, riffle height and water flow restores selectivity; simply increasing water flow may wash valuable particles away.

1.4.5 Additional functions of water

  • Provides the separating flow and carries away lighter gangue.
  • Washes out certain water-soluble impurities.
  • Suppresses dust, improving the working environment.

1.4.6 Hydraulic classifier

A hydraulic classifier sends an upward or otherwise controlled stream of water through suspended particles. The separation is based on settling velocity, which depends on density, size, shape and water velocity. Fine/light particles tend to leave in the overflow if the upward water velocity exceeds their settling velocity. Coarse/dense particles with higher settling velocities tend to move downward and leave by underflow. In force terms drag must be compared with the effective weight after buoyancy, not simply the dry weight.

Gravity separation (Wilfley table)Hydraulic classification
Main emphasis: useful specific-gravity differenceMain emphasis: settling velocity in a fluid
Inclined, vibrating riffled deck and cross-flow waterUpward or controlled stream through suspension
Dense mineral retained or guided along a different pathCoarse/dense grains settle, fine/light grains carried upward
Worked example — Hydraulic classification
At steady settling, the downward effective weight of a particle is balanced by fluid drag. In an upward water current, if the terminal settling speed exceeds the upward water speed, the particle moves downward; if it is smaller, the particle is carried upward. Size as well as density affects the separation.

1.4.7 Factors controlling separation efficiency

  • Density contrast: a larger useful contrast generally improves separation.
  • Liberation and particle size: grind sufficiently to free the ore, but avoid unnecessarily difficult ultrafine particles.
  • Water-flow rate: too little flow gives poor gangue removal; too much can carry the valuable mineral away.
  • Table inclination and vibration: tune them for stratification and transport.
  • Feed rate and riffle loading: overloading reduces selectivity.
Important: Do not infer that every oxide ore is concentrated by gravity separation. Density and settling behaviour determine whether the method is suitable.

1.5 Magnetic separation

1.5.1 Principle and operation

Either the ore or the gangue must respond differently to a magnetic field. Crushed ore travels on a conveyor belt over a magnetic pulley or roller. Magnetic particles remain attracted longer and drop nearer the roller; non-magnetic particles follow a different trajectory and are separately collected.

1.5.2 Example — cassiterite and wolframite

Non-magnetic cassiterite (SnO2) may contain magnetic wolframite-type impurities, (Fe,Mn)WO4. The magnetic impurity is removed rather than the desired mineral. Thus the valuable fraction does not have to be magnetic; the separation depends on the contrast between the fractions.

Important distinction: A magnetic separator need not collect the useful ore as its magnetic fraction. In the cassiterite–wolframite example, the magnetic impurity is removed and the non-magnetic cassiterite is retained.

Second example — chromite: Chromite, FeCr2O4 (also written FeO·Cr2O3), can be separated from non-magnetic siliceous material using a suitable magnetic field. Unlike cassiterite beneficiation, the valuable mineral is the magnetically responsive fraction.

02 Froth flotation and leaching

2.1 Froth flotation

2.1.1 Principle

Froth flotation is primarily used for sulphide ores such as galena (PbS), sphalerite (ZnS) and chalcopyrite (CuFeS2). It exploits selective differences in surface wettability. The sulphide mineral is rendered preferentially oil/collector-wet (hydrophobic), while gangue remains water-wet (hydrophilic).

2.1.2 Operation

The finely ground mineral is mixed with water and suitable reagents. Air bubbles are introduced into the agitated slurry. Collector-coated hydrophobic grains attach to the bubbles, rise and form a mineral-rich froth that is skimmed off. Hydrophilic gangue remains in the pulp and is removed in the tailings.

2.1.3 Components and their functions

ComponentFunction
WaterForms slurry or pulp; retains hydrophilic gangue
Pine oil / eucalyptus-type frotherProduces and maintains a workable dispersion of bubbles
Sodium ethyl xanthate (collector)Adsorbs on sulphide surfaces and increases hydrophobicity
Cresol / aniline (classical froth stabilisers)Improve froth persistence and limit coalescence
AirCarries hydrophobic mineral particles to the surface

Camphor oil is another traditional frother. Sodium and potassium ethyl xanthate are alternative salts of the same collector anion, C2H5OCS2−. The choice of collector, frother and pH regulator depends on the mineral surface.

2.1.4 Collector orientation — sodium ethyl xanthate

A collector has a polar or ionic end interacting with a suitable mineral surface and a non-polar hydrocarbon end tending toward a low-polarity air/oil environment. Xanthate adsorption makes the surface more hydrophobic, favouring attachment to air bubbles.

C2H5O–C(=S)–S− Na+

The sulphur-containing head binds or adsorbs on the mineral; the ethyl group is the non-polar tail. Bubble attachment reduces the energetic cost of hydrophobic mineral contact with water. The useful consequence is selective flotation, not a vague rule that similar substances simply attract.

Sodium ethyl xanthate contains a nonpolar ethyl group and a sulphur-containing polar group. Its surface affinity makes sulphide particles more hydrophobic; their attachment to air bubbles is then favoured. A frother, by contrast, controls the bubble and froth properties; the two reagents have different functions.

C2H5OCS2Na ⇌ Na+ + C2H5OCS2−Collector dissociation, schematic

2.1.5 Frothers and froth junctions

Pine oil lowers interfacial tension sufficiently to generate a stable bubble dispersion. It does not replace the collector. Thin liquid films remain at points where bubbles meet; frothers and stabilisers help prevent premature coalescence, allowing mineral-loaded froth to be removed before it collapses. Excessive froth stability is also undesirable because separation and handling become difficult.

Froth at the junction of bubbles: the bubbles are separated by thin liquid films; liquid drains through the junctions. Frother controls bubble size and delays coalescence. A mineral grain coated with collector is held at the air–water interface, reducing its contact with bulk water. An excessively persistent froth can also hinder separation and entrain unwanted fines.

2.2 Activators

An activator modifies a mineral surface so that its collector adsorbs more effectively.

2.2.1 Sulphidisation of malachite

Malachite is a basic copper carbonate, Cu2CO3(OH)2. Treatment with a sulphide reagent such as Na2S can create a copper sulphide-rich surface, allowing efficient xanthate adsorption. This illustrates that a non-sulphide ore can sometimes be floated after chemical modification of its surface.

Cu2CO3(OH)2 + 2S2− → 2CuS + CO32− + 2OH−Idealised surface sulphidisation

The equation represents conversion of the exposed copper-bearing surface into a sulphide-like surface; it does not imply that the entire ore crystal must be converted to CuS before flotation.

2.2.2 Activation of sphalerite by copper sulphate

ZnS often floats less readily than copper sulphides under comparable conditions. Cu2+ can produce a copper-rich sulphide-like layer on ZnS, improving collector adsorption. The following equation is an idealised surface exchange, not a complete description of mineral surface chemistry.

ZnS(s) + Cu2+(aq) → CuS(surface) + Zn2+(aq)

Surface reaction: Cu2+ replaces Zn2+ at the ZnS surface and forms a copper-rich sulphide layer. The layer adsorbs xanthate more effectively than the original zinc sulphide surface.

ZnS(s) + Cu2+(aq) → CuS(s) + Zn2+(aq)Simplified activation reaction

2.3 Depressants

2.3.1 Selective separation of PbS and ZnS

A depressant prevents one mineral from floating while allowing another to float. In the classical textbook separation of galena (PbS) and zinc blende (ZnS), NaCN suppresses ZnS flotation by modifying the surface and complexing zinc species. PbS remains floatable and is preferentially collected in froth.

Zn2+ + 4CN− ⇌ [Zn(CN)4]2−

Complex formation is a schematic explanation of the selective depression; actual surface chemistry is more complicated. Activation and depression are complementary methods of controlling selective flotation.

Important: Cyanide is highly toxic. The reactions are included to explain metallurgical principles, not as practical instructions.

In a mixed galena concentrate containing sphalerite and iron pyrite, the classical reagent scheme uses ethyl xanthate with cyanide and sodium carbonate to control selectivity. Carbonate helps regulate alkalinity; depression of particular sulphides depends on solution chemistry and mineral surface conditions. Do not regard sodium carbonate as a universally selective depressant.

Worked example — Separate a mixed sulphide concentrate
In the classical PbS–ZnS separation, depress ZnS so that it remains in the aqueous pulp while PbS is floated. The remaining zinc-containing fraction can subsequently be treated under suitable activation conditions. A depressant does not reduce the ore to metal; it changes its relative floatability.
Worked example — Activator versus depressant
A PbS–ZnS mixture illustrates two distinct treatments: depression suppresses collector action on ZnS during PbS flotation; subsequent activation gives the zinc mineral a more collector-responsive surface. The mineral is concentrated, not reduced, during these stages.

2.4 Chemical concentration — leaching

Leaching means selectively dissolving the desired component (or sometimes an impurity) in a suitable liquid reagent, followed by solid–liquid separation and recovery.

Powdered ore + selective leachant → dissolved species + insoluble residue

2.4.1 Examples of chemical selectivity

  • Bayer process: caustic digestion dissolves amphoteric aluminium compounds as aluminate; iron and titanium oxides largely remain in red mud.
  • Gold/silver: oxidative cyanide leaching forms soluble dicyano complexes, which can be recovered by cementation.
  • Low-grade copper ores: suitable copper compounds are leached into Cu(II) solution; copper is recovered by displacement with iron scrap or electrowinning.

The detailed individual reactions and extraction routes are explained in their respective metal sections.

Chemical concentration consists of selective dissolution, separation of insoluble residue, then recovery of the dissolved material. It is distinct from the subsequent reduction step. For example, conversion of Al(OH)3 to soluble aluminate concentrates aluminium but does not change its oxidation number.

3.2 Calcination

3.2.1 Definition and purpose

Calcination is heating of concentrated ore in absence or limited supply of air, generally below its fusion temperature. It is especially useful for carbonate and hydrated ores. It removes carbon dioxide, water and certain volatile impurities, usually forming a porous oxide. Depending on the chemistry, other sufficiently volatile components may also be removed.

3.2.2 Typical reactions

MCO3(s) → MO(s) + CO2(g)↑heat; for a suitable divalent metal carbonate
Al2O3·xH2O → Al2O3 + xH2O(g)↑heat
ZnCO3 → ZnO + CO2↑heat
FeCO3 → FeO + CO2↑idealised initial decomposition
Fe2O3·xH2O → Fe2O3 + xH2OLoss of water from hydrated iron oxide
MgCO3 → MgO + CO2Carbonate decomposition
CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)calcination; limestone
Al2O3·2H2O → Al2O3 + 2H2Oidealised bauxite formula
Worked example — Limestone mass loss
100.09 g of pure CaCO3 gives 56.08 g CaO and 44.01 g CO2. The theoretical mass loss is 43.97%.
Worked example — Mass change during calcination
For pure ZnCO3, M ≈ 125.39 g mol−1. One mole yields one mole ZnO (81.38 g) and CO2 (44.01 g). Thus 125.39 g of pure carbonate yields 81.38 g of oxide theoretically; the mass loss is about 35.1%.
Worked example — Hydrated oxide after calcination
A hydrated oxide of variable composition, Al2O3·xH2O, releases x mol water per mol of oxide formula unit. The aluminium oxidation state stays +3; the mass loss is due to release of water, not reduction of aluminium.

3.3 Roasting

3.3.1 Definition and purpose

Roasting is heating with controlled or excess air/oxygen, normally below fusion. It is commonly used for sulphide ores. Oxidation converts sulphide to oxide and, under suitable conditions, sulphate. Sulphur is often removed as SO2.

2MS + 3O2 → 2MO + 2SO2↑suitable divalent metal sulphide
2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2↑
2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2↑
PbS + 2O2 → PbSO4
4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2↑

Actual iron-sulphide roasting products depend on temperature, oxygen supply and composition. Lower oxides can also be oxidised to higher oxides.

4FeO + O2 → 2Fe2O3

3.3.2 Removal of impurities

Sulphur can leave as SO2. Arsenic and antimony may form volatile oxides such as As2O3 and Sb2O3. Organic material oxidises to CO2 and H2O. Hydrated compounds release water by thermal dehydration.

4As + 3O2 → 2As2O3Illustrative oxidation of arsenic impurity
S + O2 → SO2Illustrative removal of sulphur

Roasting products depend on temperature, oxygen supply and mineral composition: oxide, sulphate or a mixture may be formed. Volatilisation of an impurity or its oxide assists its removal. Appropriate gas treatment is essential in industrial practice.

4Sb + 3O2 → 2Sb2O3Illustrative oxidation of antimony
C + O2 → CO2Oxidation of carbonaceous matter

For an organic impurity containing carbon and hydrogen, complete oxidation produces CO2 and H2O. The oxides of arsenic and antimony can be volatile under suitable roasting conditions.

Worked example — Roasting of zinc blende
For 2 mol ZnS, 3 mol O₂ are required in the ideal oxide-forming reaction, yielding 2 mol ZnO and 2 mol SO₂. Sulphur changes from −2 to +4; zinc remains +2.

3.4 Comparison of calcination and roasting

FeatureCalcinationRoasting
AtmosphereAbsent or limited airControlled or excess supply of air/O2
Typical oreCarbonate, hydrated oxideSulphide; sometimes lower oxides
Main changeThermal decomposition; loss of CO2, H2O and volatile matterOxidation to oxide/sulphate; removal of SO2
TemperatureGenerally below fusionGenerally below fusion
ProductUsually porous oxideUsually porous oxide or a higher oxide

3.5 Porosity and sintering

Reduction is a heterogeneous solid–gas or solid–solid reaction. A porous oxide has greater accessible surface area and permits reducing gases (such as CO) to penetrate more readily. Sintering is bonding/neck formation at particle contact points, sometimes involving partial fusion and subsequent solidification. Excessive sintering closes pores and decreases accessible area; it does not create porosity. Select a thermal treatment that removes volatile products without unnecessarily destroying pore structure.

Worked example — Why avoid sintering before reduction?
When an oxide becomes porous, reducing gases reach a larger internal surface. Excessive heating can join adjacent particles at their contact points, decreasing accessible surface and hindering gas penetration. Dense sintered material and porous roasted material are therefore not equivalent for gas–solid reduction.

04 Pyrometallurgy and metal reduction

4.1 Coal, coke and carbon monoxide

Coking coal contains carbon, volatile matter and mineral impurities. Heating it in the absence of air produces coke and volatile products, including coal gas and tar. Coke has two important furnace functions: fuel to supply heat and source of the reducing atmosphere.

C + O2 → CO2strongly exothermic; supplies heat
C + CO2 ⇌ 2COendothermic Boudouard reaction

In many blast-furnace zones CO is the direct reducing gas, although coke provides the carbon source. Carbon may also participate directly in high-temperature reduction.

In a furnace, coke has different functions: it provides heat by combustion, maintains a carbon-rich reducing environment, and helps generate carbon monoxide. CO can travel through a porous oxide bed and react with the oxide. Carbon dioxide produced by reduction may react with more hot carbon to regenerate CO.

CO2 + C ⇌ 2COBoudouard equilibrium; endothermic forward reaction

4.2 Carbon reduction and smelting

Smelting is high-temperature extraction in which ore or oxide, a reducing agent and flux are heated so metal and slag phases can separate. Fe, Sn, Pb and Zn are classical examples of carbon-based reduction; the actual mechanism and physical form of the product differ.

MO + C → M + COschematic
MO + CO → M + CO2schematic

4.2.1 Examples

Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2
SnO2 + 2C → Sn + 2CO
SnO2 + 2CO → Sn + 2CO2
PbO + CO → Pb + CO2
ZnO + C → Zn(g) + CO

Zinc is obtained as vapour at typical smelting temperatures and must be condensed. For some oxides direct carbon reduction or reducing gases are unsuitable, for thermodynamic or product-quality reasons.

Fe2O3 + 3C → 2Fe + 3COidealised net direct carbon reduction
2PbO + C → 2Pb + CO2possible net carbon reduction

These are balanced net representations; gaseous CO can act as the actual reducing species in a furnace. Product gas composition is controlled by temperature and the CO/CO2 equilibrium.

Worked example — Identify oxidant and reductant
Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Fe changes from +3 to 0; carbon in CO changes from +2 to +4. Fe2O3 is the oxidising agent; CO is the reducing agent.

4.3 Flux, gangue and slag

4.3.1 Selection of flux

A flux reacts with gangue to form a fusible slag, which allows the unwanted component to be separated from the metal.

Gangue + flux → slag

Acidic gangue (e.g. SiO2) requires an appropriate basic flux (e.g. CaO). Basic oxide gangue, e.g. FeO, can require an acidic flux, SiO2.

CaCO3 → CaO + CO2heat; limestone provides lime
CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3(l)
FeO + SiO2 → FeSiO3(l)
P2O5 + 3CaO → Ca3(PO4)2formal basic slag chemistry
MgCO3 + SiO2 → MgSiO3 + CO2net carbonate decomposition and slag formation

Phosphorus(V) oxide is usually represented molecularly as P4O10; P2O5 is its empirical formula. Basic lime-rich slag can retain oxidised phosphorus. A basic magnesium-containing gangue can instead be combined with an acidic silica flux.

Worked example — Flux requirement
One mole of pure SiO₂ (about 60.08 g) requires one mole CaO (56.08 g) to produce CaSiO₃ in the ideal equation. If pure limestone supplies the lime, one mole CaCO₃ (100.09 g) is required. Real slag is a multicomponent mixture.

4.3.2 Lux–Flood acid–base concept

For oxide melts and other high-temperature systems, a Lux–Flood acid is an oxide-ion acceptor and a Lux–Flood base is an oxide-ion donor. SiO2 accepts oxide ions to form silicate; CaO provides basic oxide character. This model explains slag reactions without using an aqueous Brønsted acid–base definition.

SiO2 + O2− → SiO32−Lux–Flood acid: oxide-ion acceptor
CaO → Ca2+ + O2−Formal oxide-ion donor
Worked example — Flux selection
If the principal gangue is acidic SiO2, use a suitable basic flux (e.g. CaO). If the unwanted oxide is basic FeO, SiO2 can form FeSiO3 slag. Flux selection follows the gangue chemistry, not merely the identity of the desired metal.
CaO ⇌ Ca2+ + O2−Formal oxide-ion donor

Combining these formal Lux–Flood steps gives calcium silicate. This notation explains why silica is acidic and lime is basic in oxide melts, even when water and protons are absent.

4.3.3 Desirable properties of slag

  • Fusible and sufficiently fluid at the operating temperature.
  • Generally less dense than the molten metal so that a separate slag layer forms.
  • Capable of dissolving/retaining the targeted gangue and unwanted oxides.
  • Can shield molten metal from excessive reoxidation.

4.4 Self-reduction or auto-reduction

After partial oxidation of certain sulphide ores, the unoxidised sulphide reduces the resulting oxide or sulphate. No external carbon reducing agent is required in the decisive metal-forming reaction.

4.4.1 Lead: oxide and sulphate routes

2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2partial roasting
2PbO + PbS → 3Pb + SO2self-reduction
PbS + 2O2 → PbSO4parallel oxidation
PbSO4 + PbS → 2Pb + 2SO2self-reduction

True reducing species: in the oxide route sulphide sulphur (S2−) is oxidised from −2 to +4, losing six electrons; Pb(II) is reduced to Pb(0). Thus the sulphide is the reducing component. Copper provides another classical example (see copper extraction).

Electron accounting: In 2PbO + PbS → 3Pb + SO2, all three Pb atoms are reduced from +2 to 0 (6 electrons gained). The sulphide sulphur changes from −2 to +4 (6 electrons released). Sulphide sulphur is the true reducing species; no external carbon is needed in this reaction.

Worked example — Net lead self-reduction
Combine partial roasting, 2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2, with 2PbO + PbS → 3Pb + SO2. Cancelling 2PbO gives 3PbS + 3O2 → 3Pb + 3SO2, or PbS + O2 → Pb + SO2. The net equation hides the indispensable oxide–sulphide intermediate.
Worked example — Electron transfer in lead self-reduction
In 2PbO + PbS → 3Pb + SO2, three Pb(II) atoms collectively gain six electrons. Sulphide sulphur changes from −2 to +4, losing six electrons. Thus sulphide sulphur is the species oxidised, even though lead is reduced in both reactants.

4.5 Aluminothermic or thermite reduction

Aluminium has a very high oxygen affinity. The formation of Al2O3 is highly favourable and strongly exothermic. Aluminium can therefore remove oxygen from certain metal oxides.

Cr2O3 + 2Al → 2Cr + Al2O3
3Mn3O4 + 8Al → 9Mn + 4Al2O3
Fe2O3 + 2Al → 2Fe + Al2O3 + heat

The iron reaction is used in thermite welding. Once ignited, the reaction is strongly self-heating and may produce molten metal. Bulk iron is not ordinarily produced by thermite because aluminium is much more expensive than coke or CO for that scale of production. Titanium oxide is sometimes included in conceptual oxygen-affinity comparisons, but modern titanium is not commercially produced by simple thermite reduction of TiO2.

4.5.1 Role of ignition

A suitable high-temperature ignition system is required to initiate the strongly exothermic reaction. Historical demonstrations use energetic igniters; the igniter is not the main reducing agent. This is a study of the principle, not an experimental preparation guide.

Cr2O3 + 2Al → 2Cr + Al2O3Aluminothermic reduction
3Mn3O4 + 8Al → 9Mn + 4Al2O3Aluminothermic reduction

The stable Al–O bond and the favourable Gibbs energy of oxide formation make aluminium useful for suitable oxide reductions. The exothermic reaction still requires initiation; ignition is not a substitute for a thermodynamically feasible reduction.

Classical thermite descriptions distinguish an independent high-temperature ignition system (historically involving magnesium and oxygen-releasing materials) from the main aluminium reductant. The ignition device supplies the initial energy; the oxidation of aluminium supplies the heat of the principal reaction.

4.6 Reduction by thermal decomposition

Some relatively unstable compounds give the metal on heating.

2Ag2O → 4Ag + O2heat
2HgO → 2Hg + O2heat

In mercury extraction, cinnabar can be oxidised and mercury oxide can decompose. An idealised two-step representation is:

2HgS + 3O2 → 2HgO + 2SO2

The overall roasting reaction for cinnabar is HgS + O2 → Hg + SO2. These are pyrometallurgical operations because thermal treatment is central.

Two-stage mercury example: oxidation of cinnabar gives mercury oxide in the simplified model, then the relatively unstable HgO decomposes on heating. Mercury recovered from the hot gas is condensed. The net reaction does not require carbon.

4.7 Choosing a reduction method

The metal's chemical reactivity, stability of compounds, possible side products and the temperature govern the route. Very stable compounds of highly electropositive metals are generally reduced electrolytically; suitable moderately stable oxides can undergo carbon/CO or aluminothermic reduction; certain sulphides undergo self-reduction; unstable oxides may decompose thermally.

05 Hydrometallurgy and electrometallurgy

5.1 Hydrometallurgical reduction

Hydrometallurgy uses extraction reactions in aqueous solution. Temperature is constrained by the solvent and pressure regime, and fuel demand can be lower than in pyrometallurgy. Dissolution and separation of impurities are followed by recovery of the metal, e.g. cementation or electrowinning.

5.1.1 Cementation from cyanide complexes

A sufficiently reducing metal such as zinc displaces the noble metal from its dissolved dicyano complex, forming a soluble zinc complex.

2[Ag(CN)2]− + Zn → 2Ag + [Zn(CN)4]2−
2[Au(CN)2]− + Zn → 2Au + [Zn(CN)4]2−

Zinc is favoured in the classical treatment because it is inexpensive, sufficiently electropositive and can give rapid displacement in suitable conditions. Copper can be thermodynamically capable in particular systems; Zn is the classical choice.

5.1.2 Recovery of copper from leach liquor

Fe + Cu2+ → Fe2+ + Cu
Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu

Iron scrap supplies electrons for the reduction of dissolved Cu2+. Low-grade copper resources may therefore be processed without a conventional whole-ore smelting route.

Worked example — Metal displacement
Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu. In ionic form Fe + Cu2+ → Fe2+ + Cu. One mole of Fe transfers two moles of electrons to one mole of copper ions. The sulphate ion is a spectator in this idealised reaction.

5.2 Electrometallurgical reduction

Highly electropositive metals (Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al) form very stable compounds. Ordinary carbon reduction is not commercially convenient for these metals. Molten salts or oxides dissolved in a suitable molten electrolyte are electrolysed; in an aqueous electrolyte, hydrogen/water reduction usually occurs instead of metal deposition. The exact industrial route depends on the metal (potassium is commonly obtained by chemical reduction rather than conventional electrolysis).

5.2.1 Downs cell — extraction of sodium

Molten NaCl supplies mobile Na+ and Cl− ions. The cathode produces sodium and the anode liberates chlorine; the products must be kept separate to prevent recombination.

Na+ + e− → Na(l)cathode
2Cl− → Cl2(g) + 2e−anode
2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g)overall

A CaCl2-containing molten mixture lowers the operating temperature and improves practical flow/transport properties. A eutectic composition may melt at a lower temperature than either pure salt. The additive changes phase behaviour and transport; calling it a catalyst is incorrect merely because the melting point decreases.

The fused salt permits extraction of reactive sodium without hydrogen evolution from water. Calcium chloride lowers the operating melting temperature of the NaCl-containing mixture; it is not a catalyst. Sodium and chlorine must remain separated because they readily recombine.

Worked example — Faraday-law stoichiometry
2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). Passage of 1 F of charge theoretically deposits 1 mol Na and produces 0.5 mol Cl2, assuming 100% current efficiency.
Worked example — Why calcium chloride is not a catalyst
The molten-salt mixture has different phase behaviour from pure NaCl. CaCl2 lowers the melting range and modifies transport properties; it does not act as a conventional catalyst for the sodium-ion electrode reaction.

06 Refining of metals

6.1 Why crude metals require refining

Crude metal contains foreign metals, non-metals such as C, S, As and Sb, dissolved gases and entrained oxides or slag. Refining separates these impurities and provides the intended purity. Thermal methods remove impurities by a property difference or chemical reaction. Electrorefining achieves high purity by controlled anodic dissolution and cathodic deposition. Approximate figures such as percent-level residual impurity for thermal methods and 99.9% or greater purity for electrolytic routes are illustrative and not universal.

6.2 Poling

Poling is a classical refining method for copper and tin. It combines selective oxidation with removal of residual target-metal oxide.

6.2.1 Stage 1 — oxidation

Air is passed through molten impure metal. Impurities with higher oxygen affinity oxidise preferentially; some form volatile oxides, and others enter slag or scum. The desired metal can also oxidise to some extent.

6.2.2 Stage 2 — reduction

Once air blowing stops, green wooden poles (classical practice) or other reducing gases are used. Pyrolysis and partial combustion of the wood produce CO, hydrogen and hydrocarbons, which reduce the target-metal oxide back to metal. C, S, As and Sb are removed by oxidation/volatilisation to the extent possible. The two stages balance removal of impurities and recovery of the accidentally oxidised metal.

Cu2O + CO → 2Cu + CO2representative reaction

Poling follows an oxidation stage: oxidation is useful for removing oxidisable impurities, but may leave dissolved copper(I) oxide. The reducing stage removes the excess oxygen from the copper.

Cu2O + H2 → 2Cu + H2ORepresentative reduction by wood-derived gas

Similarly SnO2 can be reduced by a suitable reducing atmosphere. The slag/scum formed during the oxidation stage is separated; the second stage is meant to recover metal that would otherwise be lost as oxide.

6.3 Liquation or sweating

Liquation uses selective melting when the desired metal melts substantially below most impurities. Heat the impure solid on an inclined surface; the fusible metal drains away while the higher-melting impurities remain. The term sweating can vary with the exact operation. A suitable phase/melting-point difference and impurity content are necessary; an impurity threshold of 10–12% is not universal.

MetalApproximate melting point
Sn232 °C
Bi271 °C
Pb327 °C
Worked example — Liquation
A low-melting metal such as tin is separated from a suitable higher-melting solid impurity by partially melting the mixture. The liquid metal drains away, while the refractory impurity remains. Liquation relies on melting-point differences, whereas distillation relies on volatility.

6.4 Distillation

Distillation separates a volatile metal from less volatile impurities. Vaporise the desired component (or the more volatile impurity) and condense it separately.

MetalApproximate boiling point
Hg357 °C
Cd767 °C
Zn907 °C (older rounded value 920 °C)
Pb1749 °C
Fe2862 °C

For example, zinc or cadmium can be vaporised and condensed while less volatile lead and iron remain. Mercury's volatility is also used in historical refining.

Worked example — Distillation of zinc containing cadmium
Cadmium (normal boiling point about 767 °C) is more volatile than zinc (907 °C). Fractional distillation exploits this difference; less volatile lead and iron may remain behind. Actual separation depends on vapour–liquid equilibria, not a perfectly sharp temperature cut.

6.5 Zone refining — fractional crystallisation

6.5.1 Principle

Zone refining is used for ultra-purification when the impurities are preferentially soluble in the liquid phase. The distribution coefficient k is the concentration of an impurity in the solid (Cₛ) divided by its concentration in the liquid (Cₗ), at the interface.

k = Cₛ/Cₗ

If k < 1, the impurity preferentially enters the melt.

Worked example — Impurity distribution
If the distribution coefficient k = Csolid/Cliquid is 0.1, a solid crystallising in local equilibrium with liquid containing 50 ppm impurity contains about 5 ppm. When k < 1, the moving molten zone carries the preferentially liquid-soluble impurity towards one end.

6.5.2 Method

  1. Create a narrow molten zone in a solid ingot.
  2. Move the molten zone slowly along the ingot. Impurities enter the melt preferentially; purer solid crystallises behind it.
  3. Shift impurities to one end by repeated passes and remove the enriched end.

A cylindrical rod is convenient but not a fundamental requirement. The essential feature is the controlled moving liquid zone. Important examples are semiconductor/material-grade Si, Ge and Ga; related high-purity applications include In and B when their distribution coefficients permit it.

Example — why repeated zone passes help
Suppose a solid crystallises locally from a melt containing 100 ppm impurity, with k = 0.2. The local solid concentration is 20 ppm. A further pass redistributes impurity toward the end again; the enriched end is removed. The overall final purity is not simply k raised to the number of passes because the melt composition changes along the rod.

6.6 Vapour-phase refining

The metal is selectively converted into a volatile compound and then recovered by decomposition. The intermediate must be volatile and readily decomposable at an attainable temperature.

6.6.1 Mond process — nickel

Nickel reacts with CO at moderate temperature to form volatile nickel tetracarbonyl. Impurities that do not form the same volatile carbonyl remain behind. On heating the vapour, pure Ni is deposited and CO is regenerated.

Ni + 4CO ⇌ Ni(CO)4(g)50–60 °C
Ni(CO)4(g) → Ni + 4COabout 180 °C
Important: Nickel carbonyl is extremely toxic; the above is conceptual process chemistry.

6.6.2 Van Arkel–de Boer process — iodide refining

Used for highly pure titanium, zirconium and hafnium. At lower temperature a volatile metal iodide is formed. Its vapour decomposes on a hot filament (classically around 1700 K for suitable implementations). Pure metal deposits on the filament and iodine is recycled.

M + 2I2 → MI4(g)M = Ti, Zr or Hf
MI4(g) → M + 2I2hot filament

These two vapour-phase methods involve opposite steps: formation of a volatile compound under one set of conditions and its decomposition under another. The impurity does not have to volatilise. The desired metal is transported via its volatile compound and is then deposited in purified form.

6.7 Cupellation

A classical method of separating Ag or Au from readily oxidised base-metal impurities, particularly Pb. Lead forms PbO (litharge), which is absorbed in a porous cupel or removed by volatilisation depending on the setup. Noble metal is enriched because it resists oxidation.

2Pb + O2 → 2PbO

Molten lead oxide is separated from the noble-metal-rich residue; the porous cupel aids oxide removal. The important contrast is preferential oxidation of the less noble metal rather than reduction of silver or gold.

6.8 Amalgamation

Mercury forms amalgams with Ag and Au. On heating, the more volatile mercury is distilled away and the noble metal remains. Fe/Pt containers are classical examples because they do not readily form amalgams with Hg. Mercury-based processing is historically important but has severe environmental and health hazards.

Ag/Au + Hg → amalgamschematic

6.9 Electrorefining

6.9.1 Cell construction and electrode reactions

The impure metal is the soluble anode; a pure-metal starter sheet or suitable surface is the cathode. The electrolyte contains a soluble metal salt. Metal passes from the impure anode through the solution to the cathode.

M → Mn+ + ne−anode; oxidation
Mn+ + ne− → Mcathode; reduction

6.9.2 Behaviour of impurities

  • More active impurities may dissolve and remain in solution without depositing at the chosen cathode potential.
  • Noble or insoluble impurities collect below the anode as anode mud. It may contain valuable Ag, Au and platinum-group metals and is processed further.
  • Other impurities require control of the electrolyte chemistry and potential.

Faraday's law relates deposition to passed charge: m = MIt/(nF), where M is molar mass, I current, t time, n electrons per metal ion, and F Faraday constant. Under steady conditions, anodic dissolution and cathodic deposition can approximately maintain the bulk metal-ion concentration.

Worked example — Impurities in copper electrorefining
At the impure anode, copper dissolves. Copper deposits at the pure cathode. More active impurities such as suitably soluble Fe or Zn may enter solution but should not deposit under the selected conditions; less active noble impurities such as Ag and Au accumulate in anode mud.
Worked example — Electrolyte composition during refining
When the same metal dissolves anodically and is deposited cathodically at equal molar rates, the bulk metal-ion concentration can remain approximately constant. More active soluble impurities may nevertheless accumulate, while resistant noble-metal impurities can collect as anode mud.

6.10 Chromatographic separation and purification

Chromatography separates species that differ in their interaction with a stationary phase and a moving phase. In an adsorption column, a solid such as alumina retains chemical species to different extents. A suitable solvent carries the sample through the column. Less strongly retained components usually travel faster, while strongly adsorbed components emerge later.

Stages: load the sample into the column; pass the mobile phase through the stationary bed; allow separate bands to develop; collect the eluted fractions. A detector can be used to monitor fractions in an instrument. The mobile phase may be a liquid or a gas, depending on the technique.

TechniqueStationary/mobile phaseUse
Column chromatographyPacked adsorbent or other stationary material; liquid eluentSeparation of closely related soluble species
Paper chromatographyWater associated with cellulose; moving solventAnalytical separation of small samples
Gas chromatographyStationary coating or adsorbent; carrier gasVolatile, thermally suitable compounds

For metallurgical purification this usually means separating compounds, ions or complexes of elements present in small amounts, rather than pouring bulk molten metal through an adsorbent. Choice of chemical form is essential.

Worked example — Elution order
If A interacts more strongly with an alumina stationary phase than B, under the same elution conditions B normally travels ahead of A. The separation is based on unequal retention, not on melting points or density.

07 Thermodynamics of extraction — Ellingham diagram

7.1 Definition and derivation

An Ellingham diagram plots the standard Gibbs free energy of formation of oxides (or analogous compounds) against temperature. For comparison, the reactions must be normalised to the same amount of oxygen, usually one mole O2.

ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°
2M(s) + O2(g) → 2MO(s)normalised for a suitable divalent metal

The slope is approximately −ΔS° when ΔH° and ΔS° vary little with temperature within a phase region. The intercept is approximately ΔH° under that linear approximation.

7.1.1 Why most oxide lines rise

Oxygen gas is consumed to form condensed oxide, so entropy normally decreases. Thus ΔS° is negative and −ΔS° is positive. A positive slope is usual for metal-to-solid-oxide formation.

Compare all lines for the same amount of oxygen consumed, usually one mole of O2. If a reaction forms one mole of MO, it consumes only ½ mol O2; double the reaction and its ΔG° before comparison with a one-mole-O2 line. The slope is approximately −ΔS° where ΔH° and ΔS° are nearly constant.

Worked example — Read a Gibbs-energy line
If ΔH° = −400 kJ and ΔS° = −0.20 kJ K−1 per mole O2, then ΔG° = −400 + 0.20T (kJ). At 1000 K, ΔG° = −200 kJ. The line slopes upwards and crosses ΔG° = 0 at 2000 K in this simplified constant-property model.

7.1.2 Carbon oxidation lines

C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g)

Gas mole count is approximately unchanged, so ΔS° is relatively small and the line is nearly horizontal.

2C(s) + O2(g) → 2CO(g)

Gas moles increase from one to two, so ΔS° is positive and the line slopes downward. Carbon becomes useful as a reductant at high temperature when this line lies below an oxide-formation line.

7.2 Zero crossing and phase changes

7.2.1 Crossing ΔG° = 0

Where the oxide formation line crosses zero, oxide formation becomes thermodynamically unfavourable under standard-state assumptions on the positive side; the reverse decomposition becomes favourable. Classroom illustrations cite Ag2O near 300 °C and HgO near 400 °C as comparatively unstable oxides. Real decomposition depends on oxygen pressure, phase and kinetics; these are not universal decomposition temperatures.

7.2.2 Kinks in the curve

Melting, boiling and allotropy change entropy and cause a sudden change in slope. Mercury boils near 357 °C and magnesium near 1091 °C; these are examples relevant to changes in phase, not universal slope coordinates. When the metal becomes gaseous, formation of a condensed oxide may have a larger negative entropy change and steeper positive slope. The relative stability of Mg and Al oxides can depend on temperature and phase.

7.3 Criterion for reduction

At a chosen temperature, oxidation of a reducing agent must be more favourable than the corresponding formation of the oxide to be reduced. On a normalised Ellingham graph, the reductant oxidation line lies below the target metal oxide formation line. Subtract the oxide-formation reaction from the oxidation reaction of the reductant and calculate the difference in Gibbs free energy.

Fe2O3 + 2Al → Al2O3 + 2Fe
ΔG°(reaction) = ΔG°f(Al2O3) − ΔG°f(Fe2O3)

A negative value indicates thermodynamic feasibility under standard-state assumptions. It does not guarantee a rapid or industrially convenient reaction.

Worked example — Predict reduction from two oxidation lines
At a selected temperature, suppose the oxidation of M to its oxide has ΔG° = −220 kJ per mol O2 and oxidation of a reducing agent R has ΔG° = −360 kJ per mol O2. Reverse the M-oxidation reaction and add the R-oxidation reaction. ΔG°net = +220 − 360 = −140 kJ per mol O2; the reduction is thermodynamically favourable under standard conditions.

7.3.1 Carbon monoxide versus carbon dioxide

C + CO2 ⇌ 2CO

The Boudouard equilibrium shifts toward CO at elevated temperature and toward CO2/C at lower temperature. The textbook crossover around 700–710 °C is a simplified guide to comparing carbon oxidation lines. It is not a sharp universal transition in all furnaces because pressure and gas composition matter.

Above the approximate intersection of the carbon oxidation lines, near 700–710 °C for the usual standard-state comparison, formation of CO is favoured relative to the competing carbon oxidation reaction. The exact equilibrium in a working furnace also depends on gas partial pressures and carbon activity.

2CO + O2 → 2CO2CO oxidation; oxygen-normalised

At the intersection of the C/CO and C/CO2 oxidation lines, the standard Gibbs change for C + CO2 ⇌ 2CO is zero. Below the intersection CO2 is relatively favoured; above it CO is relatively favoured. To decide whether CO itself reduces MO, compare the CO-to-CO2 line with the oxide-formation line, and also consider the actual CO/CO2 pressure ratio.

7.3.2 Hydrogen as a reducing agent

2H2 + O2 → 2H2O(g)

Hydrogen can reduce oxides whose formation lines lie above the hydrogen oxidation line for the chosen conditions. CuO and PbO are readily reducible; certain Fe and Zn oxides depend on temperature and the H2/H2O partial-pressure ratio.

CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O
PbO + H2 → Pb + H2O
Worked example — Hydrogen and water vapour
For MO(s) + H2(g) ⇌ M(s) + H2O(g), assuming pure solids, Q = p(H2O)/p(H2). ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. Removing water vapour or increasing the hydrogen fraction favours reduction. The standard Ellingham line alone does not specify the actual gas composition.

Aluminium versus magnesium: compare the Al2O3 and MgO formation lines on the same per-mole-of-O2 scale at the specified temperature. Their relative positions can change with temperature and phase transitions. Do not infer a temperature-independent reduction order from a single section of an Ellingham diagram.

4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3oxide formation
2Mg + O2 → 2MgOoxide formation

Divide the first reaction and its Gibbs energy by three before comparing it with the second reaction on a one-mole-O2 basis.

7.4 Limitations

  • An Ellingham diagram predicts thermodynamic feasibility, not reaction rate, mechanism or activation barrier.
  • Standard-state lines do not automatically include activities, actual partial pressures, slag chemistry or mass transfer.
  • Carbides, intermetallics and volatile products can change the actual extraction route.
  • Phase changes and non-standard gas ratios alter practical conditions.
  • The most favourable thermodynamic reaction is not necessarily the most economical process (e.g. aluminothermy versus coke in bulk iron manufacture).

The relation ΔG° = −RT ln K links each standard reaction Gibbs energy to its equilibrium constant. For actual compositions, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. The standard graph therefore cannot, by itself, establish the reaction direction at arbitrary gas partial pressures. Analogous graphs may be drawn for sulphide or halide formation if all reactions are normalised to the same amount of the common reactant.

Worked example — Difference between two lines
For two oxygen-normalised reactions at one temperature, suppose the oxide of A has ΔG° = −650 kJ and the oxide of B has ΔG° = −420 kJ per mol O2. Oxidation of A coupled to reduction of B oxide has ΔG° = −650 − (−420) = −230 kJ per mol O2. Thus the coupled reaction is favourable in standard states.

08 Silver and gold

8.1 Silver — MacArthur–Forrest process

8.1.1 Cyanide leaching and recovery

Argentite (Ag2S) is finely powdered and treated conceptually by dilute cyanide leaching in the presence of oxygen. The metal enters solution as the dicyanoargentate(I) complex. The classroom scheme cites approximately 5% NaCN for silver; actual industrial chemistry is process-specific, and this is not an operating recommendation.

2Ag2S + 8CN− + O2 + 2H2O → 4[Ag(CN)2]− + 2S + 4OH−

Filter insoluble gangue. Zinc displaces silver from the complex.

2[Ag(CN)2]− + Zn → 2Ag + [Zn(CN)4]2−

Zinc is more electropositive, inexpensive and effective. Copper may be capable of displacement in some systems, but Zn is preferred in classical cyanidation.

In silver cyanidation the dissolved silver is present as the complex [Ag(CN)2]−, so the leaching stage is not the production of silver metal. Metal recovery follows by cementation: the more readily oxidised zinc supplies electrons and forms its cyanide complex.

An alternative way to describe silver sulphide leaching is reversible complex formation followed by oxidation of sulphide. Oxygen removes sulphide from the equilibrium, helping extraction. The precise mixture of elemental sulphur, thiosulphate and sulphate depends on the conditions; the following is an illustrative sulphate-forming net possibility.

Ag2S + 4CN− ⇌ 2[Ag(CN)2]− + S2−complexation
S2− + 2O2 → SO42−idealised complete sulphide oxidation
Ag2S + 4NaCN + 2O2 → 2Na[Ag(CN)2] + Na2SO4combined example
Worked example — Cementation electron balance
2[Ag(CN)2]− + Zn → [Zn(CN)4]2− + 2Ag. Zn(0) loses two electrons and two Ag(I) atoms each gain one electron.

8.1.2 Further purification of silver

Residual Pb is removed by cupellation. Electrorefining uses an impure Ag anode, pure Ag cathode and an acidified AgNO3 electrolyte; high purity silver is deposited at the cathode.

Ag → Ag+ + e−anode
Ag+ + e− → Agcathode

An acidified silver nitrate bath (classroom example: about 1% nitric acid) provides Ag+ for deposition; the acid helps suppress hydrolysis and maintains an acidic conducting solution. The anode dissolves Ag and the cathode collects Ag. The nitrate common ion alone is not the reason that hydrolysis is suppressed.

8.2 Parkes process — desilverisation of lead

The Ag in argentiferous lead preferentially partitions into molten zinc because it has much greater solubility/affinity for the zinc-rich phase than for the lead-rich phase. The distribution coefficient K = [Ag] in Zn-rich phase / [Ag] in Pb-rich phase is qualitatively much greater than one.

  1. Add molten zinc to silver-bearing molten lead. The zinc-rich and lead-rich phases separate under suitable conditions.
  2. Ag migrates preferentially into the zinc-rich phase. On cooling, a Zn–Ag-rich crust separates and floats owing to phase/density behaviour.
  3. Skim the crust; zinc is removed/recovered by distillation (boiling point approximately 907 °C, older rounded 920 °C).
  4. Purify the residual silver-rich material by cupellation and/or electrorefining.

Parkes refining is based on liquid-phase partitioning, not on electrolysis. Silver preferentially enters the zinc-rich phase of the lead melt. The separated zinc-rich material is subsequently processed to recover silver and remove zinc. The lead-rich phase has lower silver content.

Pattinson method (historical alternative). On cooling a dilute liquid Pb–Ag alloy in the lead-rich region of its phase diagram, lead-rich crystals form first. Removing these crystals enriches silver in the remaining liquid. Repeated fractional crystallisation concentrates Ag before final separation and refining. This process is distinct from Parkes, which introduces Zn and relies on partitioning between phases.

Worked example — Compare silver enrichment methods
Parkes: add zinc and collect the silver-rich zinc phase; remove zinc by distillation. Pattinson: cool the Pb–Ag melt and remove lead-rich crystals repeatedly. Cupellation: oxidise remaining lead to PbO.
Worked example — Why zinc-rich crust removes silver
For a qualitative distribution coefficient K = [Ag]Zn-rich/[Ag]Pb-rich much greater than 1, silver preferentially enters the zinc-rich phase. Cooling and physical separation therefore remove silver from lead before the zinc is recovered by distillation.

8.3 Gold — cyanide leaching

Low-grade auriferous quartz is crushed and leached conceptually using dilute aerated cyanide (the classroom scheme cites about 0.5% NaCN). Gold forms dicyanoaurate(I). The oxidation half-reaction and overall Elsner equation are:

Au + 2CN− → [Au(CN)2]− + e−
4Au + 8CN− + O2 + 2H2O → 4[Au(CN)2]− + 4OH−
2[Au(CN)2]− + Zn → 2Au + [Zn(CN)4]2−cementation
Worked example — Why oxygen is needed for gold leaching
The formal oxidation half-reaction is Au + 2CN− → [Au(CN)2]− + e−. Oxygen is the electron acceptor in the overall aerated leach; subsequent cementation reduces Au(I) to Au(0). Complex formation and redox are coupled.

8.4 Purification of crude gold

8.4.1 Acid treatment

Removes zinc and some base metals.

8.4.2 Cupellation

Residual Pb is oxidised to PbO and removed.

2Pb + O2 → 2PbO

8.4.3 Borax treatment

Borate flux helps transfer oxidised base-metal impurities such as copper to slag.

2Cu + O2 → 2CuO
CuO + B2O3 → Cu(BO2)2simplified borate slag representation

8.4.4 Parting

Concentrated sulphuric acid selectively dissolves silver as Ag2SO4 while gold remains.

2Ag + 2H2SO4(conc.) → Ag2SO4 + SO2 + 2H2O
2Ag + 2H2SO4 → Ag2SO4 + SO2 + 2H2OConcentrated acid; historical parting chemistry

Gold is retained in the residue because it does not readily dissolve in this oxidising acid alone. The silver compound is separated; the noble-metal-rich residue is purified further.

8.4.5 Final electrorefining

Refining can yield gold of 99.99% purity or higher, depending on the process. Cyanide and acid chemistry here is intended only for study of redox, coordination and industrial extraction principles.

The chloride-based Wohlwill electrorefining principle uses impure Au as the anode, a pure Au cathode and an acidic gold chloride electrolyte, commonly represented by HAuCl4 in HCl. Gold is transported as chloride complexes.

Au + 4Cl− → [AuCl4]− + 3e−formal anode reaction
[AuCl4]− + 3e− → Au + 4Cl−formal cathode reaction

8.5 Applications of silver and gold

MetalApplicationProperty or chemical basis
SilverElectrical contacts, plating and reflective coatingsHigh electrical conductivity and reflectivity
SilverHistorical photographic films and papersLight-sensitive silver halides
SilverCoins, ornaments and silverwareMalleability; Cu alloying improves hardness
SilverSome medical dressings and historical dental amalgamsSilver-containing materials have specialised antimicrobial or restorative uses
GoldJewellery, precision electrical contacts and coatingsCorrosion resistance and ductility

Silver nitrate can produce dark marks through formation of finely divided silver or other silver compounds. Its historical use in marking inks and certain formulations is a chemical example, not a recommendation for skin application.

09 Extraction of tin

9.1 Cassiterite and its concentration

Cassiterite (SnO2) may occur in low-grade material containing only a few percent SnO2. Important impurities include silica/silicates, Fe/Cu sulphides and magnetic wolframite, (Fe,Mn)WO4.

  1. Gravity separation or levigation: enrich dense SnO2 from lighter gangue.
  2. Controlled roasting: oxidise Fe/Cu sulphides to soluble sulphates where possible and remove some volatile impurities.
  3. Hot-water washing: remove soluble iron and copper sulphates.
  4. Magnetic separation: remove magnetic wolframite from non-magnetic cassiterite. The enriched product is the black tin concentrate.

A tin concentrate may still contain iron and copper sulphides after gravity and magnetic treatment. Roasting can change susceptible sulphide impurities to soluble sulphates, which can be washed away. This is selective chemical removal of impurities before the cassiterite reduction stage.

FeS + 2O2 → FeSO4Idealised sulphating roasting of an iron sulphide impurity
CuS + 2O2 → CuSO4Idealised sulphating roast, under suitable conditions

Soluble sulphates are removed with water. The desired cassiterite is not appreciably soluble in that washing step; hence the chemical treatment increases the grade without reducing Sn(IV).

Sulphating roasting may convert iron and copper sulphide impurities into water-soluble sulphates; some oxide particles remain and can be removed by subsequent physical washing. Magnetic separation can be performed before or after suitable thermal treatment, depending on the flowsheet.

CuS + 2O2 → CuSO4illustrative sulphating roasting

A classical enriched black-tin concentrate is quoted at about 60–70% SnO2; actual concentrate grades vary.

9.2 Smelting reactions

Coke supplies heat and carbon monoxide; carbon and CO reduce tin oxide. Limestone provides a basic flux to remove silica.

C + O2 → CO2
C + CO2 ⇌ 2CO
SnO2 + 2C → Sn + 2CO
SnO2 + 2CO → Sn + 2CO2
CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3(l)
SnO2 + C → SnO + COpartial reduction
SnO + C → Sn + COfurther reduction

Anthracite or coke supplies the reducing carbon in the classical reverberatory-furnace route (approximately 1500 K in the teaching example). Lime is used when siliceous impurities require a basic flux.

Worked example — Tin yield
Pure SnO₂ has molar mass about 150.71 g mol⁻¹. Complete reduction yields one mole of Sn, about 118.71 g. The maximum theoretical mass of tin from 100 g of pure cassiterite is therefore 78.77 g.

9.3 Tin loss in slag and recovery

SnO/SnO2 can interact with silica. A schematic representation for tin(II) silicate formation is:

SnO + SiO2 → SnSiO3

Some tin therefore enters slag. Tin-bearing slag is re-smelted with carbon and flux to recover additional tin.

Loss of tin to slag decreases recovery. Tin-bearing slag can be reprocessed under suitable reducing conditions; all of the tin in the original ore does not necessarily enter the first metal product.

SnSiO3 + CaO + C → Sn + CaSiO3 + COslag retreatment; schematic
SnSiO3 + Fe → Sn + FeSiO3alternative schematic slag retreatment

The first equation represents transfer of silica to a calcium-containing slag while carbon removes oxygen. The second represents iron reducing tin(II) species, with iron passing into a silicate phase. Real slags contain mixtures rather than pure stoichiometric silicates.

Worked example — Tin oxide carried into slag
Tin silicate formation lowers metal recovery because tin is incorporated in the slag instead of being collected in the metal phase. Re-smelting an appropriate slag with carbon and flux can recover part of the tin; separation by slag formation must not be confused with complete removal of valuable metal.

9.4 Refining tin

Liquation first separates the low-melting tin from less fusible impurities. Poling removes oxidisable impurities and reduces remaining metal oxide. For very high purity, electrorefining in an acidic soluble tin-salt electrolyte deposits pure tin at the cathode.

Sn → Sn2+ + 2e−soluble anode model
Sn2+ + 2e− → Sncathode

For the classical soluble-anode electrorefining model, the electrolyte is SnSO4 in dilute H2SO4. The crude tin anode supplies Sn(II) and a pure tin cathode receives the metal.

10 Extraction of magnesium

10.1 Preparation of magnesium chloride

Extraction of magnesium is organised into three stages: obtain purified hydrated MgCl2, convert it to anhydrous MgCl2 without hydrolysis, and electrolyse the fused salt.

10.1.1 From carnallite

Carnallite, KCl·MgCl2·6H2O, is dissolved and fractionally crystallised. Under suitable conditions KCl crystallises preferentially, leaving MgCl2-rich liquor. Concentration and crystallisation yield purified MgCl2·6H2O.

10.1.2 From seawater — Dow process

Lime precipitates dissolved magnesium as magnesium hydroxide. The precipitate is treated with hydrochloric acid to obtain magnesium chloride solution, which is purified and concentrated.

Mg2+ + Ca(OH)2 → Mg(OH)2↓ + Ca2+
Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl → MgCl2 + 2H2O

Seawater contains dissolved Mg2+ on the order of grams per litre, not 65 ppm MgCl2.

Seawater composition: seawater contains dissolved Mg2+ of the order of grams per litre, not tens of ppm as a universal MgCl2 concentration. Lime treatment precipitates Mg(OH)2; the magnesium hydroxide is recovered separately and converted to MgCl2.

10.1.3 From magnesite

Magnesite is MgCO3. Calcination first removes CO2 and gives MgO. Carbothermal chlorination converts the oxide to chloride, which can then be electrolysed.

MgCO3 → MgO + CO2calcination
MgO + C + Cl2 → MgCl2 + COidealised chlorination

Direct carbothermal reduction of MgO is possible only under demanding high-temperature, low-pressure conditions and requires control of reverse oxidation of Mg vapour. It is not the usual fused-chloride route.

MgO + C ⇌ Mg(g) + CO(g)high temperature; low pressure, conceptual

10.2 Dehydration without hydrolysis

Direct heating of hydrated magnesium chloride promotes hydrolysis, giving basic chloride and eventually magnesium oxide. A dry HCl-containing atmosphere suppresses the hydrolysis equilibrium.

MgCl2 + H2O ⇌ MgOHCl + HCl
MgOHCl → MgO + HClon further heating

An alternative high-temperature route uses chlorination of suitable magnesium oxide in the presence of carbon. Analogous chlorination chemistry is used for other refractory oxides; products depend on thermodynamics and conditions.

MgO + C + Cl2 → MgCl2 + CO
2MgO + C + 2Cl2 → 2MgCl2 + CO2Alternative overall carbon-assisted chlorination representation

It is essential to distinguish hydrated chloride from anhydrous chloride. Heating hydrated MgCl2 under unsuitable conditions causes hydrolysis to basic chloride or oxide; simply evaporating all the water does not guarantee dry MgCl2.

MgCl2·6H2O → MgCl2 + 6H2Odehydration in HCl-containing atmosphere
MgCl2·6H2O → MgO + 5H2O + 2HClnet hydrolysis on strong heating

In seawater the total magnesium content is approximately 0.13% by mass, not the mass percentage of anhydrous MgCl2. Magnesium is present as dissolved ions associated with chloride, sulphate and other anions.

Worked example — Why dehydration is a chemical problem
MgCl2·6H2O cannot simply be treated like every hydrated salt: the chloride can hydrolyse as water is removed. Formation of MgOHCl and subsequently MgO lowers the amount of usable anhydrous chloride. A suitable HCl-containing atmosphere suppresses hydrolysis, while alternative chlorination routes regenerate chloride.

10.3 Electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride

A classroom composition is MgCl2:NaCl ≈ 4:1; actual molten salt mixtures vary. Sodium chloride lowers melting point and improves practical conductivity/flow.

Mg2+ + 2e− → Mg(l)cathode
2Cl− → Cl2(g) + 2e−anode
MgCl2(l) → Mg(l) + Cl2(g)overall

Molten Mg is less dense than the salt mixture and floats; it must be protected from oxidation or burning by a controlled inert or reducing atmosphere. Historical accounts mention coal gas. Aqueous electrolysis is unsuitable because water is preferentially reduced.

A representative historical cell contains MgCl2, NaCl and CaCl2 in a molten bath, around 973–1023 K in the classroom account. Graphite serves as the chlorine-evolving anode, and the steel or iron cathode receives magnesium. Further purification may use vacuum distillation, exploiting the volatility of magnesium under reduced pressure.

Worked example — Magnesium chloride electrolysis
Mg2+ + 2e− → Mg; 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−. Thus 1 mol Mg and 1 mol Cl2 correspond to 2 F of charge at 100% current efficiency.

10.4 Thermal reduction of dolomite — Pidgeon process

Dolomite, CaMg(CO3)2, is first calcined. The resulting mixture of CaO and MgO is reduced by the silicon component of ferrosilicon. Calcium oxide binds the oxidised silicon in the calcium silicate residue. A low magnesium vapour pressure drives the equilibrium toward metal formation; magnesium vapour is then condensed separately.

CaMg(CO3)2 → CaO + MgO + 2CO2calcination
2MgO + 2CaO + Si → 2Mg(g) + Ca2SiO4silicothermic reduction; ferrosilicon supplies Si

The process is typically discussed around 1100–1200 °C under reduced pressure. Iron in ferrosilicon is largely a carrier component, not the main reductant. Unlike the Dow process, this route need not convert MgO into MgCl2.

Worked example — Role of lime and vacuum
Silicon is oxidised to silicate. CaO stabilises the solid calcium silicate product; continual removal of Mg vapour lowers its partial pressure and helps shift the equilibrium toward magnesium.

11 Extraction and refining of aluminium

11.1 Bauxite composition and beneficiation

Bauxite is a heterogeneous ore rich in gibbsite, Al(OH)3, boehmite and diaspore, AlO(OH), with Fe2O3, SiO2 and TiO2 impurities. The older formula Al2O3·2H2O is an approximate shorthand, not a unique bauxite composition.

Red bauxite contains appreciable iron oxide, giving reddish-brown colour. White/pale bauxite has lower iron content but may be richer in silica. Silica dissolves in strong alkali and can consume both caustic and alumina, so silica-rich material can require different pretreatment.

11.2 Bayer process — purification of bauxite

11.2.1 Step 1 — caustic digestion

Conditioning or calcination may depend on mineralogy. Strong NaOH (about 40% in the classroom description) dissolves amphoteric Al(OH)3 as soluble aluminate. Iron and titanium oxides remain largely in the solid red mud under Bayer conditions.

Al(OH)3 + OH− → [Al(OH)4]−
Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O → 2Na[Al(OH)4]

Silica can also react with hydroxide to produce silicate and subsequently sodium aluminosilicate products; this consumes alkali and alumina and explains why high-silica ore is troublesome.

SiO2 + 2OH− → SiO32− + H2O

Bauxite is a mixture of hydrated aluminium oxides, not a compound of a single fixed hydration state. Amphoteric aluminium hydroxide dissolves in hot alkali as aluminate. Iron-rich residue is separated from the liquor; silica may also react with alkali and can complicate the separation.

SiO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2OIdealised silicate formation

The traditional red-bauxite classroom route includes oxidation of FeO where present, followed by digestion near 150 °C under pressure (the example gives 8 atm). These are illustrative conditions; actual Bayer digestion depends strongly on whether the alumina-bearing mineral is gibbsite, boehmite or diaspore.

4FeO + O2 → 2Fe2O3oxidative pretreatment, if required

11.2.2 Step 2 — clarification

Separate the insoluble red mud from the soluble sodium aluminate liquor by solid–liquid separation.

11.2.3 Step 3 — precipitation of aluminium hydroxide

Controlled dilution/reduced causticity and seeding promote precipitation. In the textbook CO2 model, carbon dioxide neutralises OH− and shifts the aluminate equilibrium toward solid Al(OH)3.

[Al(OH)4]− → Al(OH)3↓ + OH−
CO2 + 2OH− → CO32− + H2O

Fine Al(OH)3 seeds provide nuclei, accelerating controlled crystal growth and shortening induction time. Excess mineral acid can redissolve amphoteric Al(OH)3 as Al3+, so strong acid addition is not the preferred strategy in this scheme.

Dilution and seeding favour precipitation of aluminium hydroxide from purified aluminate liquor. In the alternative carbonation representation, CO2 consumes alkalinity and promotes precipitation. Excess acid must not be confused with controlled precipitation: amphoteric Al(OH)3 also dissolves in sufficiently acidic solution.

Worked example — Precipitation and amphoterism
Reducing the effective hydroxide concentration shifts aluminate toward Al(OH)3 precipitation. Seed crystals supply nucleation surfaces. Excess strong acid can dissolve the precipitated hydroxide again; therefore acidification is not equivalent to controlled precipitation.

11.2.4 Step 4 — calcination

2Al(OH)3 → Al2O3 + 3H2Oheat

The product is purified alumina. The modern sequence is Bayer alumina production followed by Hall–Héroult reduction.

Worked example — Alumina yield from aluminium hydroxide
2Al(OH)3 → Al2O3 + 3H2O. About 156 g of pure Al(OH)3 yields about 102 g of Al2O3 theoretically. This is dehydration, not reduction; Al remains in oxidation state +3.

11.3 Hall process — historical alkali fusion

Fuse bauxite or alumina-bearing material with sodium carbonate. Leach the water-soluble sodium aluminate, filter out insoluble impurities, precipitate Al(OH)3 and calcine it. Silica also reacts in this route, which causes contamination and material loss for silica-rich ore.

Al2O3 + Na2CO3 → 2NaAlO2 + CO2
SiO2 + Na2CO3 → Na2SiO3 + CO2

In the historical carbonate-fusion scheme, aqueous sodium aluminate liquor is warmed (approximately 50–60 °C in the classroom example) and carbon dioxide precipitates aluminium hydroxide while sodium carbonate is regenerated.

2NaAlO2 + CO2 + 3H2O → 2Al(OH)3 + Na2CO3carbonation, simplified molecular equation

11.4 Serpek process — historical silica-rich bauxite route

At high temperature, carbon and nitrogen convert alumina to aluminium nitride. Silica is carbothermically removed in the historical teaching model; actual Si-containing products depend on furnace conditions.

Al2O3 + 3C + N2 → 2AlN + 3CO

The nitride is hydrolysed and the hydroxide calcined.

AlN + 3H2O → Al(OH)3 + NH3
2Al(OH)3 → Al2O3 + 3H2O
SiO2 + 2C → Si + 2COSimplified carbothermic silica-removal model

Historical descriptions use high-temperature removal of silica-derived products; their actual form may include other volatile silicon species depending on conditions. In contrast, the alumina is deliberately converted to AlN, which is hydrolysed rather than directly reduced to aluminium.

A historical Serpek teaching temperature is about 1800 °C. The hydrolysis stage releases NH3, a recoverable coproduct. This is chemically different from the electrolytic reduction stage, which produces aluminium metal.

11.5 Hall–Héroult process — electrolytic reduction

11.5.1 Cell construction and electrolyte

The carbon-lined steel tank acts as cathode and consumable graphite/carbon blocks as anodes. Alumina is dissolved in a molten cryolite-rich bath; CaF2 modifies properties. The historical classroom mixture is 60% cryolite, 20% CaF2, 20% alumina; industrial composition is not fixed at these numbers. Alumina is replenished continuously.

Cryolite (Na3AlF6) dissolves alumina and lowers operating temperature compared with pure alumina. CaF2 adjusts fluidity, melting behaviour and conductivity. Graphite conducts electricity and tolerates high temperature, but the anodes are consumed chemically/electrochemically during operation.

11.5.2 Electrode and overall reactions

Al3+ + 3e− → Al(l)formal cathode representation
2O2− → O2 + 4e−formal anode step
C + O2 → CO2
2Al2O3 + 3C → 4Al + 3CO2net representation

Some CO can also form. Carbon anodes are gradually oxidised and must be replaced. Molten Al collects at the cathode region. A historical carbon/coke covering reduces radiative heat loss and helps shield the hot bath from air; it does not stop consumption of immersed anodes.

C(s) + O2− → CO(g) + 2e−formal carbon anode reaction
C(s) + 2O2− → CO2(g) + 4e−formal carbon anode reaction

The bath operates near 950 °C in typical classroom descriptions. A traditional practical illustration is about 0.5 kg of consumed carbon per kg of aluminium, exceeding the ideal CO2-only stoichiometric requirement. Carbon losses depend on operating conditions.

Worked example — Charge and anode consumption
The cathode requires 3 mol electrons per mol Al. For the idealised CO2-only overall equation, 4 mol Al require 3 mol C. Actual carbon consumption is greater or otherwise affected by side reactions and cell efficiency.
Worked example — Ideal alumina and carbon consumption
For 2 mol Al₂O₃ (about 203.92 g), the ideal CO₂-only reaction yields 4 mol Al (107.93 g) and consumes 3 mol C (36.03 g). Therefore theoretical consumption per kg aluminium is about 1.89 kg alumina and 0.334 kg carbon, before accounting for losses and side reactions.

11.5.3 Why not use aqueous aluminium salts or simple molten AlCl3?

In ordinary aqueous aluminium salt solutions, water/H+ is reduced in preference to Al3+. Anhydrous AlCl3 is molecular/covalent and volatile; it sublimes readily, so simple fused AlCl3 is not a convenient ionic electrolyte on its own. A molten fluoride bath containing dissolved alumina is the industrial solution.

11.6 Hoopes process — three-layer electrolytic refining

The three molten layers are density-engineered to remain separate.

  • Bottom: dense impure Al alloyed with a heavier metal (classically Cu), serving as anode.
  • Middle: molten fluoride electrolyte containing aluminium species; BaF2 may be used to adjust its density.
  • Top: pure molten aluminium, serving as cathode.
Al → Al3+ + 3e−lower anode
Al3+ + 3e− → Alupper cathode

Pure aluminium accumulates in the upper layer and may reach approximately 99.99% purity. The density difference is central to maintaining separate layers. Covering the furnace reduces oxidation and contamination.

The separation is sustained by the density ordering of the three liquids. Impure aluminium is present in the dense lower alloy layer, the fluoride electrolyte lies in the middle, and pure aluminium forms the lighter upper layer. The two metal layers are separated by the conducting electrolyte. The anode dissolves aluminium as Al(III), while the upper cathode receives the purified metal.

The three liquid layers themselves serve as the electrode phases and electrolyte. External electrical contacts are still necessary; the phrase “no electrodes” is not literally correct. A carbonaceous covering can limit heat loss and screen glare from the hot surface.

Worked example — Three layers in Hoopes refining
The impure aluminium alloy must be denser than the electrolyte, which must in turn be denser than pure molten aluminium. If the density order fails, the layers cannot remain separated and cathodic purification becomes ineffective.

11.7 Comparison of aluminium processes

StageProcessKey chemistry
Ore purificationBayerAmphoteric dissolution and seeded precipitation
Historical purificationHallAlkali fusion to sodium aluminate
Historical silica-rich routeSerpekAlN formation, hydrolysis and calcination
Metal productionHall–HéroultMolten fluoride electrolysis of dissolved alumina
Metal refiningHoopesThree-layer electrolytic transfer

11.8 Applications of aluminium

ApplicationReason
Foil and packagingEasily rolled into thin sheets; useful barrier properties
Electrical transmissionGood conductivity relative to mass
Aircraft and transport alloysLow density and suitable strength when alloyed
