Paints and metallic coatingsFine aluminium flakes provide reflective effects
Aluminothermic reductionStrong affinity for oxygen makes Al a useful reductant for selected oxides

Aluminium is protected by an adherent oxide film under many ordinary conditions, despite being a strongly reducing metal thermodynamically.

12 Extraction of lead

12.1 Galena beneficiation

Galena (PbS) is often associated with ZnS and siliceous gangue. Selective flotation with a NaCN-type depressant suppresses ZnS so that PbS concentrates. Two broad routes are described: carbon/smelting for lower-grade or gangue-rich concentrate, and self-reduction for cleaner sulphide concentrate after controlled partial roasting.

12.2 Roasting and side products

2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2
PbS + 2O2 → PbSO4

Roasting conditions control the fraction of oxide/sulphate. Silica can react undesirably with lead oxide to produce lead silicate and metal loss. Small lime additions influence sulphate/silicate and slag behaviour.

PbO + SiO2 → PbSiO3schematic loss

The roasting stage can generate both PbO and PbSO4. Depending on the route chosen, these products are reduced with carbon/CO or react with unroasted PbS. Roasting everything to oxide would remove the sulphide required by the self-reduction route.

Worked example — Why lime is mentioned in galena roasting
Siliceous material can bind lead oxide into unwanted lead silicates, reducing recovery. In the classical scheme, small lime additions modify slag chemistry and help manage problematic sulphate/silicate formation. This is distinct from the later PbS–PbO self-reduction reaction.

12.3 Carbon reduction and smelting

Carbon or CO reduces lead oxide. Lime and iron-oxide/flux chemistry assist the removal of impurities to the slag; calcium silicate is a classical teaching component of lead slag.

PbO + C → Pb + CO
PbO + CO → Pb + CO2
CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3

12.4 Self-reduction

Unroasted PbS reduces the roasted PbO/PbSO4, yielding metallic lead.

2PbO + PbS → 3Pb + SO2
PbSO4 + PbS → 2Pb + 2SO2
Worked example — Sulphate–sulphide route
PbSO4 + PbS → 2Pb + 2SO2. Sulphate sulphur changes +6 → +4 and gains 2 e−; sulphide sulphur changes −2 → +4 and loses 6 e−; two Pb(II) atoms gain 4 e−. Total gained = total lost = 6 electrons.

12.5 Refining crude lead

Oxidative softening (historical settnering-type treatment) removes As, Sb, Sn and other impurities as oxides/scum. If silver is appreciable, the Parkes process desilverises lead. Electrorefining produces high-purity Pb when required.

Betts electrorefining: impure lead forms the soluble anode and purified lead is deposited on the cathode. The classical electrolyte contains lead(II) hexafluorosilicate, PbSiF6, and hexafluorosilicic acid, H2SiF6. Organic additives such as gelatin modify deposit quality. The process can give around 99.95% or higher purity, depending on operation.

Pb → Pb2+ + 2e−anode
Pb2+ + 2e− → Pbcathode

Liquation separates low-melting lead from higher-melting components where applicable. Oxidative softening and Parkes desilverisation address other specific impurities before or instead of final electrorefining.

13 Extraction of copper

13.1 Chalcopyrite constitution and concentration

Chalcopyrite CuFeS2 is a compound, not a mechanical mixture of Cu2S, FeS and FeS2. A common formal oxidation-state representation is Cu+Fe3+(S2−)2. Matte chemistry is nevertheless conveniently discussed in terms of Cu2S and FeS. Concentrate the ore by froth flotation.

Copper mineralFormulaClass
Chalcopyrite (copper pyrites)CuFeS2Sulphide
Chalcocite (copper glance)Cu2SSulphide
Cuprite (ruby copper)Cu2OOxide
MalachiteCu2CO3(OH)2Basic carbonate
AzuriteCu3(CO3)2(OH)2Basic carbonate

Copper may also occur natively. Sulphide concentrates are commonly processed pyrometallurgically; suitable low-grade oxide ores and some sulphide ores can be leached. The older classroom threshold of about 4% copper for dry processing is not a universal industrial cutoff.

13.2 Roasting

Iron sulphide oxidises preferentially because Fe has a higher oxygen affinity under the relevant conditions; much copper remains as Cu2S. A little Cu2O can form and may react with residual FeS to return copper to the sulphide matte.

2FeS + 3O2 → 2FeO + 2SO2
Cu2O + FeS → Cu2S + FeO

FeS can transfer sulphur to the copper oxide, retaining copper in the sulphide matte while FeO becomes available for slag formation. Chalcopyrite is not a mechanical mixture of Cu2S, FeS and FeS2; these components help represent subsequent matte chemistry.

2CuFeS2 + O2 → Cu2S + 2FeS + SO2idealised partial oxidation
2As2S3 + 9O2 → 2As2O3 + 6SO2illustrative impurity oxidation
2Sb2S3 + 9O2 → 2Sb2O3 + 6SO2illustrative impurity oxidation

13.3 Smelting — matte formation

Coke supplies heat. Acidic silica flux removes FeO as fusible ferrous silicate slag. The molten copper matte consists mainly of Cu2S and FeS. Direct carbon reduction of the sulphides is not the desired route; iron preferentially enters slag as oxide.

FeO + SiO2 → FeSiO3(l)

Matte is a molten sulphide-rich intermediate, not pure copper. Iron sulphide is selectively oxidised to iron oxide; silica removes FeO as iron silicate slag. Copper remains largely in the sulphide-rich matte until conversion.

13.4 Bessemer converter

13.4.1 Stage 1 — iron removal

Air is blown through molten matte with silica. FeS is oxidised to FeO, which reacts with silica. Pour off the iron-rich slag after removal of FeS. Historical flame observations are qualitative process indicators.

2FeS + 3O2 → 2FeO + 2SO2
FeO + SiO2 → FeSiO3
Worked example — Why iron removal precedes copper self-reduction
FeS has a stronger oxygen affinity under the converter conditions and is oxidised to FeO. Silica converts FeO into iron-silicate slag. Removing the slag leaves a copper-rich sulphide phase for partial oxidation and subsequent self-reduction.

13.4.2 Stage 2 — copper self-reduction

Part of the remaining Cu2S is oxidised to Cu2O. The oxide reacts with unoxidised sulphide to produce copper. SO2 gas escapes and causes cavities/blisters upon cooling; blister copper classically contains about 98–99% Cu.

2Cu2S + 3O2 → 2Cu2O + 2SO2
2Cu2O + Cu2S → 6Cu + SO2
Worked example — Self-reduction stoichiometry
2Cu2O + Cu2S → 6Cu + SO2. Six copper(I) atoms gain a total of six electrons, while sulphide sulphur loses six electrons. The escape of SO2 through solidifying copper causes the blistered appearance.
Worked example — Copper conversion balance
Combine 2Cu₂S + 3O₂ → 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂ with 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂. Cancelling Cu₂O gives the net equation 3Cu₂S + 3O₂ → 6Cu + 3SO₂. Of three stoichiometric formula units of Cu₂S, two are oxidised to the oxide intermediate.

13.5 Refining blister copper

Poling reduces residual dissolved copper oxide. Electrorefining uses an impure copper anode, pure copper cathode and acidified CuSO4 electrolyte. Ag, Au and platinum-group metals can report to anode mud; high-purity electrolytic copper is deposited.

Cu → Cu2+ + 2e−anode
Cu2+ + 2e− → Cucathode

Electrorefining can give copper of approximately 99.99% purity in suitable industrial practice. Anode dissolution and cathode deposition transfer copper through the electrolyte while impurity behaviour is controlled by electrode potentials and electrolyte chemistry.

Air blowing oxidises residual sulphur and arsenic; oxidised iron forms removable scum or slag. Poling subsequently reduces copper(I) oxide using reducing gases from wood or controlled modern alternatives.

Cu2O + CO → 2Cu + CO2poling
4Cu2O + CH4 → 8Cu + CO2 + 2H2Opoling, idealised methane reaction

Fe, Zn, Ni and Co may enter the acidified electrolyte as soluble ions during electrorefining; noble impurities such as Ag and Au tend to remain in anode slime. Their exact distribution depends on electrolyte and electrode potentials.

13.6 Hydrometallurgical extraction of copper

In contrast with matte smelting, hydrometallurgy brings copper into a soluble ionic form before recovering it. Sulphide heaps can undergo slow oxidative leaching aided by air, water and microbial activity; carbonate and oxide copper ores can react with acid. Historical descriptions mention leaching over many months, but rates depend on ore mineralogy and process design.

CuFeS2 + 4O2 → CuSO4 + FeSO4simplified oxidative leaching balance
2Cu2S + 5O2 → 2CuSO4 + 2CuOidealised partial oxidation
CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2Ooxide leaching
Cu2CO3(OH)2 + 2H2SO4 → 2CuSO4 + CO2 + 3H2Omalachite acid leaching

Copper-bearing liquor can be processed by cementation with iron or by solvent extraction followed by electrowinning. The simple displacement reactions illustrate the electron-transfer principle.

CuSO4 + Fe → FeSO4 + Cucementation
CuSO4 + Zn → ZnSO4 + Cualternative displacement
Cu2+ + H2 → Cu + 2H+hydrogen reduction under suitable conditions
Worked example — Recover copper from a leach solution
One mole of Fe supplies two electrons to one mole of Cu(II). Under ideal complete cementation 55.85 g Fe can recover 63.55 g Cu.

13.7 Uses and alloys of copper

MaterialPrincipal constituentsApplication
CopperCuWires, cables and electrical conductors; plating
BrassCu + ZnFittings and machined articles
BronzeCu + SnBearings, casting and ornaments
Bell metalCu–Sn, generally relatively tin-richBells and resonant castings
GunmetalCu–Sn–ZnCast valves and fittings
German silver / nickel silverCu–Ni–Zn; contains no AgDecorative articles and hardware

Copper and copper alloys are also used in coins, jewellery and corrosion-resistant components. Exact alloy compositions vary with the grade.

14 Extraction of zinc

14.1 Ores and concentration

Calamine (smithsonite, ZnCO3 in the classical scheme) is a carbonate ore. Zinc blende or sphalerite (ZnS) is a sulphide ore frequently associated with galena and siliceous gangue. Selective/double froth flotation, using depressant and activator control, enriches ZnS.

14.2 Thermal preparation

14.2.1 Calamine route

ZnCO3 → ZnO + CO2calcination

14.2.2 Zinc blende route

2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2roasting

At unsuitable lower or particular temperatures ZnSO4 can form. Higher-temperature roasting decomposes sulphate; the classroom temperature range is roughly 800–900 °C or above, not a universal decomposition threshold.

ZnS + 2O2 → ZnSO4
2ZnSO4 → 2ZnO + 2SO2 + O2heat

The oxidation product is governed by roasting conditions. Zinc sulphate formed at some stages can decompose at higher temperature to zinc oxide, so the roasting stage prepares the oxide for subsequent reduction.

At sufficiently elevated temperatures (roughly 800–900 °C in the classroom model), zinc sulphate decomposes towards ZnO. The desired furnace feed is oxide, not sulphate or sulphide.

14.3 Carbon smelting and vaporisation

The historical classroom furnace temperature is approximately 1300–1400 °C. Zinc vapour is produced because the operating temperature is above zinc's normal boiling point (907 °C). Volatile cadmium may accompany it; the zinc is condensed as crude spelter.

ZnO + C → Zn(g) + CO

Coke also maintains a reducing atmosphere, consuming CO2 that could otherwise reoxidise the zinc. The classical Ellingham interpretation prefers direct carbon reduction as the net high-temperature route rather than treating ZnO + CO → Zn + CO2 as the isolated preferred overall reaction; actual reduction depends on gas composition and equilibrium.

C + CO2 ⇌ 2CO
Zn(g) + CO2 ⇌ ZnO + COPossible reverse oxidation

Excess carbon consumes CO2 through the Boudouard equilibrium, helps maintain a low local oxygen potential, and limits this reverse reaction. The escaping zinc-containing vapour is cooled separately to recover spelter.

In the older vertical-retort process, a mixture of zinc oxide and coke may be formed into briquettes with a binder. Zinc-containing vapour leaves the heated retort and enters a condenser, while solid residues remain behind. A classroom reduction temperature of 1673 K (about 1400 °C) is consistent with recovery of zinc as vapour.

14.4 Refining of spelter

Crude zinc may contain Cd, Fe, Pb and other impurities. At about 800 °C more volatile cadmium (bp ≈ 767 °C) can be removed preferentially. At or above zinc's boiling point, zinc is distilled away from high-boiling Fe/Pb and condensed.

14.4.1 Electrolytic refining and electrowinning

Use suitable zinc sulphate electrolyte; zinc is deposited on a removable sheet. Aluminium cathode sheets permit stripping of zinc and are common in electrolytic zinc production. Distinguish a soluble-anode electrorefining model from industrial zinc electrowinning, which commonly uses an insoluble anode.

Zn2+ + 2e− → Zncathode
Zn → Zn2+ + 2e−soluble anode in electrorefining

High-purity zinc (about 99.99%) can be obtained electrolytically. Deposited zinc does not simply redissolve in the acidic bath during proper cathodic operation, because the imposed cathodic potential favours deposition. Its ordinary reaction with dilute acid is separate.

Zn + H2SO4(dil.) → ZnSO4 + H2

The electrolyte is generally an acidified aqueous zinc sulphate solution in conventional zinc electrowinning. Distinguish electrowinning from electrorefining: electrowinning obtains metal from a dissolved compound, whereas electrorefining transfers metal from an impure anode to a pure cathode.

Worked example — Theoretical zinc deposition
Zn2+ + 2e− → Zn. 2 F theoretically deposit 1 mol Zn, about 65.38 g, at 100% current efficiency.
Worked example — Electrode reaction versus acid dissolution
The ordinary chemical reaction Zn + H2SO4(dil.) → ZnSO4 + H2 oxidises metallic zinc. At the working cathode, electrical energy drives the opposite metal-ion half-reaction, Zn2+ + 2e− → Zn. The two descriptions refer to different conditions.

14.5 Applications of zinc

UseUnderlying principle
Galvanising ironZinc forms a protective coating and can sacrificially corrode in preference to iron
Dry cells and batteriesZn commonly serves as the negative electrode (anode during discharge); in a traditional zinc–carbon cell the can is zinc
Brass and nickel silverAlloy formation with Cu and, for nickel silver, Ni
Recovery of Ag and AuZn displaces noble metals from suitable dissolved complexes
Chemical reductionZinc dust and activated Zn-containing reagent systems act as reductants
Worked example — Why galvanised iron is protected
The zinc coating provides a barrier. If a small scratch exposes iron in a conducting wet environment, zinc can oxidise preferentially and provide sacrificial protection.

15 Extraction of iron

15.1 Iron ores and preparation

Ore/mineralFormula or representationComment
HaematiteFe2O3Principal high-grade iron ore
MagnetiteFe3O4Magnetic iron ore
Limonite / hydrated oxideFe2O3·xH2O (approx.)Hydrated mixture, not fixed composition
SideriteFeCO3Carbonate ore

After concentration, calcination/roasting converts material largely toward a suitable oxide-rich charge. Hydrated oxide loses water; siderite decomposes and FeO can oxidise to Fe2O3. Excessive FeO can react with silica and cause Fe loss into slag.

FeCO3 → FeO + CO2heat
4FeO + O2 → 2Fe2O3
Fe2O3·xH2O → Fe2O3 + xH2O
FeO + SiO2 → FeSiO3

15.2 Blast furnace

15.2.1 Charge and counter-current operation

The burden consists of iron oxide/sinter/pellets, coke and limestone/dolomite flux. A traditional educational mass ratio for roasted ore:coke:limestone is 8:4:1; actual proportions depend on the ore grade, coke quality and flux demand. The charge descends from the top while hot reducing gases ascend from lower regions. Hot air enters via tuyeres. The distribution of temperatures is approximate and varies with furnace operation.

15.2.2 Combustion and reducing gas formation

In the hot tuyere/combustion region coke reacts with oxygen to release heat. CO2 then reacts with carbon to generate CO. Classical teaching diagrams assign roughly 1500–2000 °C to the hottest combustion region; locally the temperature can exceed that range.

C + O2 → CO2
CO2 + C ⇌ 2CO

15.2.3 Reduction zone

CO is the main direct reducing gas in upper and middle furnace regions. In a suitable temperature/oxygen-potential range, iron oxides are progressively reduced: Fe2O3 → Fe3O4 → FeO → Fe. The classroom diagram cites about 500–800 °C for the reduction region; wüstite is not stable at all temperatures and direct reduction also occurs at higher temperature.

3Fe2O3 + CO → 2Fe3O4 + CO2
Fe3O4 + CO → 3FeO + CO2
FeO + CO → Fe + CO2
Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2overall

In the cooler reduction region the resulting iron may remain porous and solid (often called sponge iron in the teaching description) before it descends, carburises and melts. Excess CO and removal of CO2 favour reduction; the Boudouard equilibrium helps establish the CO/CO2 ratio.

Fe2O3 + CO → 2FeO + CO2balanced net intermediate reduction, where FeO is stable
Worked example — Sequential reduction of iron oxide
3Fe2O3 + CO → 2Fe3O4 + CO2; 2Fe3O4 + 2CO → 6FeO + 2CO2; 6FeO + 6CO → 6Fe + 6CO2. Adding gives 3Fe2O3 + 9CO → 6Fe + 9CO2. Divide by three to obtain the overall equation.
Worked example — Iron oxide reduction
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. One mole of pure Fe₂O₃ yields two moles Fe (111.69 g) theoretically. Thus 100 g of Fe₂O₃ can yield approximately 69.94 g of iron, before industrial losses.

15.2.4 Calcination, flux and slag

Limestone decomposes to CaO; CaO reacts with acidic silica to form calcium silicate-rich slag. The classical diagram uses about 800–1000 °C for the slag-formation region; actual melting and reactions are spread across zones.

CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3(l)
Worked example — Limestone needed for silica removal
CaCO3 → CaO + CO2; CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3. In this idealised stoichiometry, one mole of CaCO3 provides CaO for one mole of SiO2. About 100 g pure limestone is needed theoretically for 60 g pure silica. Actual slag has multiple components.

15.2.5 Hearth and tapping

Molten pig iron collects at the bottom beneath the less-dense slag. Metal and slag are tapped separately. The slag layer helps protect the metal and carries gangue impurities away.

Fusion zone: the descending iron absorbs carbon, lowering its melting temperature. Liquid iron and slag trickle into the hearth, where the less dense slag floats above iron and provides some protection against reoxidation. Classroom descriptions often place fusion near 1200–1300 °C and the hotter combustion region near 1500–1600 °C; these bands are approximate and do not represent universal industrial furnace temperatures.

15.3 Why pig iron contains impurities

Molten iron at high temperature dissolves carbon and can take up elements formed by reduction of other oxides in the bosh/hearth. Under strongly reducing conditions silica and manganese oxides undergo reduction and phosphates can introduce phosphorus.

SiO2 + 2C → Si + 2CO
Mn3O4 + 4C → 3Mn + 4CO

Pig iron contains appreciable carbon (typically around 3.5–4.5% in the classical representation), Si, Mn, P, S and other impurities. It is hard and brittle relative to low-carbon wrought iron/steel.

Worked example — Origin of impurities in pig iron
The hot reducing region can reduce silica and manganese oxides, so Si and Mn may enter the iron. Carbon dissolves in molten iron; phosphorus may enter from reduced phosphate species. Hence obtaining elemental Fe from its oxide does not by itself guarantee pure iron.

15.4 Blast-furnace by-products

Calcium silicate-rich slag is used in cement, aggregate and ballast, depending on composition. A representative dry/top-gas composition is roughly N2 58%, CO 25%, CO2 10%, H2 6.5% (illustrative; real gas composition varies). CO and H2 provide fuel value. Cleaned gas can be reused in heating.

16 Steelmaking, alloying and heat treatment

16.1 From pig iron to steel or wrought iron

The common metallurgical principle is oxidation of excess C, Si, Mn, P and other impurities, removal as gas or slag, and controlled addition of carbon and alloying elements to obtain desired properties. Sulphur removal also depends on appropriate slag chemistry and refining conditions.

16.1.1 Puddling

A historical oxidising treatment using an iron-oxide-rich lining or charge. Iron oxide participates as oxygen carrier. Oxidation/refining lowers impurities to produce wrought iron.

During oxidative puddling, impurities in pig iron, including carbon, silicon, manganese and sulphur, are reduced in amount by oxidation and slag-forming processes; iron oxide can act as an oxygen carrier. The metal is refined into low-carbon iron. Sulphur removal also depends on slag chemistry.

FeO + C → Fe + COOxygen transfer to carbon
2FeO + Si → 2Fe + SiO2Idealised oxidation of silicon
FeO + Mn → Fe + MnOIdealised oxidation of manganese

16.1.2 Bessemerisation

Air is blown through molten iron to oxidise excess impurities. An acid Bessemer converter has a silica lining and requires low-phosphorus feed because it cannot remove phosphorus effectively.

Si + O2 → SiO2oxidation
2Mn + O2 → 2MnOoxidation
MnO + SiO2 → MnSiO3schematic acidic slag

The historical pear-shaped converter has a refractory lining selected for slag chemistry. An acidic silica lining is unsuitable for effective phosphorus removal; a basic lining and lime-rich oxidising slag are needed for the Thomas route.

16.1.3 Basic Bessemer or Thomas process

A basic CaO/MgO/dolomite lining allows oxidised phosphorus to be retained in phosphate slag.

3CaO + P2O5 → Ca3(PO4)2

Thomas slag was historically used as fertiliser.

Worked example — Acid and basic Bessemer comparison
A silica-lined converter is unsuitable for efficient phosphorus removal. A basic lining allows oxidised phosphorus to be incorporated into phosphate slag. This is an application of acidic oxide–basic flux chemistry.

16.1.4 Open-hearth process

Historical slow oxidative refining with better compositional control than early Bessemer processing.

16.1.5 LD or basic oxygen process

High-purity oxygen replaces air, producing rapid oxidation/refining with much less nitrogen pickup. This improves the quality and weldability of suitable steels compared with early air-blown processing.

16.2 Carbon content and steel classes

ClassClassroom carbon mass %Broader approximate range / properties
Mild or low-carbon0.15–0.30%About 0.05–0.30%; ductile and weldable
Medium-carbon0.30–0.60%Higher strength and hardness
High-carbon0.60–0.80%About 0.60–1.0%; hard and wear-resistant
Tool steel0.80–1.4%Many grades about 0.8–1.5% with alloying; cutting/wear uses

These are educational ranges; boundaries vary by steel standard and actual alloy composition.

Form of ironApproximate classroom C mass %Properties
Wrought ironAbout 0.1–0.25 in older teaching ranges; modern wrought iron often lowerSoft, ductile, fibrous slag inclusions
SteelAbout 0.25–2 (older convention); many low-carbon steels contain lessProperties depend on composition and heat treatment
Cast ironAbout 2.5–4.3Good castability; often brittle
Pig ironAbout 2.3–4.6 (classroom range); typically around 3–4.5Blast-furnace product containing C and other impurities

Increasing carbon generally increases hardness potential and decreases ductility at comparable processing conditions. Wrought iron generally melts at a higher temperature than high-carbon cast iron; alloys melt across ranges, so a fixed melting point order is only a broad classroom trend.

16.3 Alloy additions and deoxidation

Spiegeleisen is a historical Fe–Mn–C alloy. Addition after excessive oxidation can restore the required C/Mn content and assist deoxidation. Ferromanganese, ferrosilicon and ferrochrome introduce Mn, Si and Cr respectively; ferrosilicon is a deoxidiser. Ferroalloys can provide more homogeneous dissolution and better composition control than elemental powders.

FeO + Mn → Fe + MnOManganese as deoxidiser
2FeO + Si → 2Fe + SiO2Silicon as deoxidiser

Alloying additions and deoxidising additions serve related but different purposes. Deoxidation removes dissolved oxygen or oxide inclusions by forming more stable oxides; controlled alloying adjusts the properties of the finished metal.

16.4 Heat treatment of steel

Annealing, quenching and tempering differ in temperature–time history and the resulting microstructure. The comparison below is qualitative; the following subsections explain each treatment.

16.4.1 Annealing

Heat steel to a suitable austenitising or recrystallisation range (classroom value about 700–800 °C) and cool slowly. Annealing softens steel, improves workability and relieves internal stresses; specially annealed low-carbon alloys have magnetic/electrical applications.

16.4.2 Quenching or hardening

Heat to an appropriate temperature and cool rapidly in water, oil or brine. In suitable steels this produces a hard but brittle martensitic structure.

16.4.3 Tempering

Reheat quenched steel at a lower temperature (classroom example 200–300 °C) and cool in a controlled way. Tempering reduces brittleness while retaining useful hardness and toughness.

The new theory notes quote tempering around 500–575 K (227–302 °C), as one example for quenched steels. Annealing and hardening may involve heating to the appropriate transformation range followed by slow cooling or quenching respectively. The critical temperature varies with composition; a universal 700–800 °C rule is not valid for every grade.

Worked example — Choose a heat treatment
A cold-worked steel part requiring improved ductility: anneal. A suitable steel tool requiring high hardness: harden by quenching. A quenched component requiring lower brittleness while retaining useful hardness: temper. Exact cycles depend on the alloy and required microstructure.

16.5 Surface or case hardening

The objective is a hard, wear-resistant surface while the interior retains toughness/ductility.

16.5.1 Carburising

Enrich the surface of low-carbon steel in carbon at elevated temperature, then quench suitably. The carbon-rich case hardens while the core remains tougher.

16.5.2 Cyaniding and carbonitriding

Historical cyaniding introduces both C and N into the surface. Modern carbonitriding is a related controlled surface-enrichment route. Cyanide-based treatment is hazardous and tightly regulated.

16.5.3 Nitriding

Suitable nitride-forming alloy steels, for example Al-containing steels, are heated in an ammonia atmosphere (classroom range about 500–550 °C). Hard nitrides form near the surface and improve wear resistance. Applications include machinery and drilling components.

Case hardening produces a hard surface with a comparatively tough core. Carburising enriches the surface in carbon; nitriding enriches it in nitrogen; carbonitriding introduces both. It is not equivalent to making the entire component uniformly high in carbon.

Example: aluminium in a suitable nitriding steel forms hard nitride precipitates. The nitrogen-enriched surface is wear resistant without requiring the entire component to be made of high-carbon steel. This differs from carburising, where carbon enrichment is followed by an appropriate hardening treatment.

16.6 Complete iron-to-steel relationship

Iron ore → oxide preparation → blast furnace → pig iron → oxidative refining → controlled C/alloy content → heat treatment → steel for the intended application

16.7 Applications of iron and steel

MaterialTypical applications
Cast ironDrainage pipes, stove castings, machine bases
Wrought iron (historical)Chains, anchors, agricultural implements, forged items
Low-carbon steelSheets, structural shapes and formed parts
Nickel steelTough components and specialised structural alloys
Chromium or alloy tool steelsCutting tools, wear-resistant machinery
Stainless steelUtensils, corrosion-resistant equipment and transport components

Carbonitriding and carburising are used for wear-resistant components such as gears and certain axles, with a tough core. Alloy and heat treatment selection determines whether a steel can meet the intended load, wear and corrosion demands.

17 Reaction chemistry, redox and nitric acid

17.1 Classes of inorganic reactions

Ion-exchange/metathesis (including precipitation), acid–base, complexation, redox and thermal decomposition are important reaction classes. Metallurgical processing often combines several of these. A precipitation reaction removes an ion by formation of an insoluble solid; oxidation and reduction alter oxidation states; complexation can selectively change solubility and stability.

17.2 Ion exchange and precipitation

17.2.1 Lithopone — double-precipitation pigment

BaS + ZnSO4 → ZnS↓ + BaSO4↓

The white mixture of ZnS and BaSO4 is lithopone, historically used as a white pigment. Basic lead carbonate (white lead) darkens in H2S because black PbS forms. Lithopone resists this particular blackening mechanism much more effectively.

Pb2+ + H2S → PbS↓ + 2H+blackening

17.2.2 Peroxide oxidation of black lead sulphide

PbS + 4H2O2 → PbSO4 + 4H2O

Black PbS becomes white PbSO4. Sulphur is oxidised from −2 to +6; peroxide is reduced. The colour change is useful in redox reasoning.

Worked example — Colour and oxidation state
PbS is black; PbSO4 is white. In oxidation by peroxide, Pb stays at +2 while S changes from −2 to +6, giving the eight-electron oxidation. Four H2O2 molecules accept eight electrons in the overall equation.

17.2.3 Precipitate conversions and solubility

PbCl2 + Na2S → PbS↓ + 2NaCl

White/sparingly soluble PbCl2 becomes black PbS.

PbCl2 + 2NH4OH → Pb(OH)2↓ + 2NH4Clclassroom molecular representation

PbCl2 is sparingly soluble in cold water but substantially more soluble in hot water. Silver halide colours: AgCl white, AgBr pale yellow/cream, AgI yellow.

Ag+ + Cl− → AgCl↓White
Ag+ + Br− → AgBr↓Cream
Ag+ + I− → AgI↓Yellow

17.3 Disproportionation and comproportionation

Disproportionation occurs when the same element in one oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. Comproportionation occurs when different oxidation states of a single element converge to an intermediate oxidation state.

17.3.1 Halogens with alkali

For chlorine, bromine and iodine, with important kinetic and side-reaction differences:

X2 + 2OH− → X− + XO− + H2Ocold dilute alkali; hypohalite
3X2 + 6OH− → 5X− + XO3− + 3H2Ohot concentrated alkali
5X− + XO3− + 6H+ → 3X2 + 3H2Oacidification; comproportionation

The stability of individual hypohalites varies; iodine hypoiodite disproportionates readily. For bromine in hot alkali and the subsequent acidification specifically:

3Br2 + 6OH− → 5Br− + BrO3− + 3H2O
5Br− + BrO3− + 6H+ → 3Br2 + 3H2O
Worked example — Halogen oxidation numbers
X2 + 2OH− → X− + XO− + H2O. One halogen atom is reduced 0 → −1, another oxidised 0 → +1. For the chlorate-type equation, one atom oxidised to +5 balances the reduction of five atoms to −1.

17.3.2 Phosphorus in alkali

P4 + 3OH− + 3H2O → PH3↑ + 3H2PO2−

P(0) disproportionates to P(−3) in phosphine and P(+1) in hypophosphite. Phosphine is gaseous and escapes. Acidifying the remaining hypophosphite solution therefore does not simply regenerate the original phosphorus by reverse comproportionation.

17.4 Extraction and purification of sulphur

17.4.1 Frasch process

Three concentric pipes are used in classical underground sulphur extraction. Superheated water melts underground sulphur; compressed air assists the lifting of molten sulphur to the surface. Modern industrial importance varies with region and resource type.

17.4.2 Alkaline purification and recovery

In the classical chemical purification model, sulphur reacts with alkali to produce soluble sulphide and thiosulphate species. Insoluble gangue is removed; acidification of the combined sulphur species can recover elemental sulphur.

4S + 6OH− → 2S2− + S2O32− + 3H2O
2S2− + S2O32− + 6H+ → 4S↓ + 3H2Ooverall idealised recovery

Speciation depends on conditions. The reaction is a theoretical description, not an operational recipe.

17.5 Manganate(VI) disproportionation

Green manganate MnO42− is unstable when the medium is not sufficiently alkaline. Mn(VI) disproportionates to Mn(VII) and Mn(IV).

3MnO42− + 2H2O → 2MnO4− + MnO2↓ + 4OH−

MnO4− is purple permanganate, and MnO2 is brown/black. Decreasing hydroxide drives the displayed equilibrium forward. The precise products and their stability depend on pH and redox conditions.

17.6 Comproportionation of sulphur species

2H2S + SO2 → 3S↓ + 2H2O

S(−2) in hydrogen sulphide and S(+4) in sulphur dioxide converge to elemental S(0). Aqueous SO2 is often represented as H2SO3 (hydrated sulphur dioxide) in elementary schemes; its actual speciation is equilibrium-dependent.

Worked example — Sulphur oxidation-number balance
In 2H2S + SO2 → 3S + 2H2O, two sulphur atoms at −2 lose four electrons in total and the sulphur atom at +4 gains four electrons. The three atoms reach oxidation state zero.

17.7 Copper(I) disproportionation / comproportionation

Copper has common oxidation states +1 and +2. In simple aqueous solution, Cu+ tends to disproportionate.

2Cu+ ⇌ Cu2+ + Cu

The opposite reaction is favoured if Cu+ is selectively stabilised or removed from the solution. Ligands such as Cl−, Br−, I−, CN−, SCN− and S2O32− may stabilise Cu(I) by poorly soluble salts or complexes, depending on conditions.

Cu + Cu2+ ⇌ 2Cu+comproportionation when Cu(I) is sufficiently stabilised
Worked example — Cu(I) stability
2Cu+ ⇌ Cu2+ + Cu. Cu(I) acts as both oxidant and reductant in this disproportionation. Selective stabilisation of Cu(I) by a ligand or precipitate can change the thermodynamic preference; the behaviour of free aqueous Cu+ is not universal for all Cu(I) compounds.

17.8 Oxidising and non-oxidising acids

HCl (dilute or concentrated) and dilute H2SO4 are typically non-oxidising acids in these comparisons: H+ acts as the oxidising species for active metals. Concentrated H2SO4 and HNO3 can also act as oxidants through sulphur(VI) and nitrogen(V) species.

17.8.1 Zinc examples

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2↑
Zn + H2SO4(dil.) → ZnSO4 + H2↑
Zn + 2H2SO4(conc.) → ZnSO4 + SO2↑ + 2H2O

The first two reduce H+; the third reduces sulphur from +6 to +4.

17.9 Metal reactions with nitric acid

17.9.1 Concentrated acid

Concentrated HNO3 commonly gives NO2 with many metals.

Cu + 4HNO3(conc.) → Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O
Ag + 2HNO3(conc.) → AgNO3 + NO2 + H2O

17.9.2 Dilute acid

Copper with dilute nitric acid (e.g. the classroom ~20% example) commonly yields NO. NO can subsequently be oxidised by air to brown NO2.

3Cu + 8HNO3(dil.) → 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O
2NO + O2 → 2NO2

17.9.3 Dependence of nitrogen product on reaction conditions

NO2, NO, N2O, N2 and NH4+ (including NH4NO3 with sufficiently active metals under suitable conditions) can be formed. Which product predominates depends on metal, concentration, temperature and other reaction conditions. These are trends rather than a universal stoichiometric rule.

Worked example — NO versus NO₂
For Cu with dilute HNO3, the commonly taught NO equation is 3Cu + 8HNO3 → 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O. With concentrated HNO3, Cu + 4HNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O. These are typical outcomes, not an unconditional prediction for every metal and acid concentration.

Electron accounting for nitrate reduction: nitrogen is +5 in nitrate, +4 in NO2, +2 in NO, +1 on average in N2O, 0 in N2 and −3 in NH4+. The electron demand increases as the nitrogen oxidation state decreases.

NO3− + 2H+ + e− → NO2 + H2O
NO3− + 4H+ + 3e− → NO + 2H2O
2NO3− + 10H+ + 8e− → N2O + 5H2O
2NO3− + 12H+ + 10e− → N2 + 6H2O
NO3− + 10H+ + 8e− → NH4+ + 3H2O

These balanced half-reactions are electron-balance tools, not predictions of a unique product under all conditions.

Worked example — Why nitrate product changes electron demand
Three Cu atoms oxidised to Cu²⁺ release six electrons. Two nitrate ions reduced to NO consume six electrons. If the nitrate product were NO₂ instead, six nitrate ions would consume those same six electrons. Additional nitrate ions act as counterions in copper nitrate.

17.9.4 Tin with nitric acid

Very dilute nitric acid may give soluble Sn(II) salts and highly reduced nitrogen products; under concentrated nitric acid tin is oxidised toward hydrated Sn(IV) oxide (metastannic acid in classical descriptions), represented approximately as H2SnO3 or SnO2·xH2O, not a simple stable Sn(NO3)4 solution. Specific dilute-acid products are condition-dependent.

Sn + 4HNO3(conc.) → H2SnO3 + 4NO2 + H2Oidealised hydrated oxide representation

17.9.5 Passivation

Fe, Cr and Al become passive in concentrated nitric acid owing to a compact protective surface film that suppresses continued reaction. Suitable aluminium-containing equipment can therefore be compatible with concentrated nitric acid under controlled industrial conditions. Passivation is conditional and does not imply universal resistance at all concentrations.

17.10 Concentrated nitric acid with non-metals and metalloids

Strong oxidation produces higher oxidation-state oxyacids/oxides; NO2 is a common nitrate-reduction product under concentrated conditions.

ElementTypical oxidation product

C + 4HNO3(conc.) → CO2 + 4NO2 + 2H2O

Representative balanced equations for additional oxidation products:

B + 3HNO3 → H3BO3 + 3NO2

These equations use NO2 as the representative reduction product of concentrated nitric acid; actual products and hydration may depend on conditions.

17.12 Conceptual examples with solutions

17.12.1 Example 1 — phosphorus on acidification

Question: Why are phosphorus disproportionation products not simply converted back to elemental phosphorus on acidification?

Explanation: PH3 produced in alkaline disproportionation is gaseous and leaves the medium. The hypophosphite ion remains; the reduced partner is no longer available to reverse the redox process. This contrasts with the idealised sulphur purification model, where both dissolved sulphur species can react on acidification.

17.12.2 Example 2 — manganate and pH

Question: Why does green manganate change colour below strongly alkaline pH?

Explanation: Lower hydroxide concentration favours disproportionation of Mn(VI) into purple MnO4− and brown-black MnO2. The net reaction generates OH−, so consumption of OH− drives it forward.

3MnO42− + 2H2O → 2MnO4− + MnO2↓ + 4OH−

17.12.3 Example 3 — bromine, alkali and acidification

Question: What happens when Br2 reacts with hot concentrated NaOH and the resulting solution is acidified?

Explanation: Bromide and bromate are formed. Their oxidation states, −1 and +5, converge to Br2 on acidification.

3Br2 + 6OH− → 5Br− + BrO3− + 3H2O
5Br− + BrO3− + 6H+ → 3Br2 + 3H2O

17.12.4 Example 4 — zinc with hydrochloric and sulphuric acids

Question: Compare Zn with concentrated HCl and concentrated H2SO4.

Explanation: HCl supplies H+ as the oxidising species and H2 forms. Concentrated H2SO4 can reduce sulphur(VI) to SO2 while oxidising zinc.

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2
Zn + 2H2SO4(conc.) → ZnSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O

17.12.5 Example 5 — copper and nitric acid concentration

Question: What is the nitrogen-containing product when Cu reacts with ~20% HNO3? How does it compare with concentrated acid?

Explanation: Dilute acid commonly gives NO, whereas concentrated acid commonly gives brown NO2, subject to the actual reaction conditions. NO may turn brown on contact with air because it oxidises to NO2.

17.12.6 Example 6 — tin and nitric acid

Question: Contrast tin with very dilute, dilute and concentrated HNO3.

Explanation: Very dilute acid can yield soluble Sn(II) compounds and strongly reduced nitrogen products such as ammonium ions. In dilute acid, oxidation and nitrate-reduction products depend on the conditions; do not assign a unique product merely from the word dilute. Concentrated acid produces hydrated Sn(IV) oxide, often described as metastannic acid, with nitrogen oxide evolution.

17.12.7 Example 7 — stabilising Cu(I)

Question: When is Cu + Cu2+ ⇌ 2Cu+ driven forward?

Explanation: A ligand or precipitating ion that selectively stabilises Cu(I) or removes Cu+ from solution can shift the equilibrium toward Cu(I). Examples include suitable halides, CN−, SCN− or thiosulphate under appropriate conditions.

17.12.8 Example 8 — sulphur extraction and purification

Question: Describe the Frasch process and the alkaline route for purification.

Explanation: Superheated water melts underground sulphur and compressed air helps lift it to the surface through concentric pipes. In the classical chemical purification scheme, soluble sulphide and thiosulphate are formed, insoluble gangue is separated, and idealised acidification brings the sulphur species back toward elemental sulphur.
